nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say GNN in conversation and in papers, and spell out the full term when introducing it. You will hear it in data science, machine learning and research talks. Outside technical settings the phrase is rarely used.

distinctions.note: A CNN works on grid-like data such as images, while a graph neural network works on nodes and edges with irregular connections.
Graph embedding is a general way to map graph elements to vectors, while a GNN is a trained neural architecture that does this with learning.

collocations: message passing in graph neural networks
node classification with a graph neural network

examples.everyday: My friend who works on recommendation systems says her team uses a graph neural network for that.
examples.professional: We switched the fraud model to a graph neural network so it can use the links between accounts.
examples.analytical: A graph neural network encodes relational structure by letting each node update its representation from its neighbors.

nuance.analogy: It is like a group of people in a social network who each update their opinion by listening to their direct friends, then repeating this several times.
nuance.etymology: Combines 'graph' from Greek 'graphein' (to write) with 'neural network' from the model of biological neurons.
common_mistakes: Saying 'graph' with a vowel like 'graf' only in one spelling, or confusing it with 'graft'.
Using 'graph network' as a shorter name without 'neural', which can mean a different thing.

conversation.text: A graph neural network updates each node's representation by aggregating messages from its neighbors.
We used a graph neural network to predict properties of molecules from their bond structure.

senses.definition: A tombstone or other permanent fixed object to indicate the location of a grave.
senses.example: We placed a simple grave marker with my grandfather's name at the old country cemetery.

core.definition: An object, such as a headstone or plaque, that shows where a person is buried and often gives the name and dates.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MARK, not on GRAVE. The final -er is a weak, reduced syllable, and the r is pronounced clearly in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical, used in cemetery, military or official contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say headstone or gravestone for the stone itself, and grave marker when speaking generally or officially. The Department of Veterans Affairs provides grave markers for eligible veterans, so the term appears often in government and cemetery paperwork. In casual talk, people usually say the headstone.

distinctions.note: A headstone is the upright stone at the head of a grave and is the most common everyday term for the marker.
Gravestone means nearly the same thing and is common in everyday speech, while grave marker is more general and official.
A monument is usually larger and may commemorate a person or event, while a grave marker is a small, practical object for one burial.

examples.everyday: The cemetery office said the grave marker for my dad will be installed next month.
examples.professional: The cemetery district needs the design of the grave marker approved before the crew can start the installation.
examples.analytical: A grave marker expresses a community's memory, since it tells passersby that a particular life once mattered to someone.

nuance.analogy: A grave marker is like a street sign for the dead, telling visitors exactly where to find a person.
nuance.etymology: Grave comes from Old English græf; marker is formed from the verb mark with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on GRAVE instead of MARKER.
Saying grave marker as two separate words without linking them in natural speech.

senses.definition: Praises what someone said.

core.definition: A phrase used to praise what someone just said, meaning that is a very good or valid point.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on POINT, and great is said with a light, quick primary sound. Link the t of great smoothly into the p of point without a pause.

nuance.connotation: Positive, a friendly way to agree and show appreciation in a discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in meetings, group chats and casual conversations to acknowledge a good idea. Good point is even more common and sounds slightly more natural in many offices, so great point works best when you really want to show enthusiasm. Respond with thanks or add to the idea, such as Thanks, or Let me build on that.

distinctions.note: Good point is the most common version and is slightly more neutral; great point signals stronger enthusiasm.
I agree states your position; great point praises the specific comment that was made.

examples.everyday: My neighbor said we should plant tomatoes later in the spring, and I told her, great point, the frost is still a risk.
examples.professional: During the sprint review, Priya said we should test the model on older data, and I replied, great point, let's add that to the plan.
examples.analytical: Mill's objection to the argument is a great point, since it shows that the premise depends on an unstated assumption about consent.

nuance.analogy: It works like a thumbs-up in spoken form: it confirms that the other person landed a good hit.
nuance.etymology: Great comes from Old English great, large or important; point comes from Latin punctum, a dot or prick.
common_mistakes: Using great point to mean a physical great point or a geographic point: the phrase is only for praising an argument or comment.
Pronouncing point with a short vowel as pent; the American vowel is the diphthong in joint.

conversation.text: Great point. We hadn't thought about the holiday traffic.
That's a great point, Priya. Let's add it to the list.
Great point about the costs; I'll update the slide.

senses.definition: In a greedy manner; with keen or ardent desire.
senses.example: The two dogs greedily devoured the meat.

core.definition: In a way that shows a strong, eager desire to have or consume as much as possible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GREE. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final -ly is a clear ee sound, not a long i.

nuance.connotation: Negative, usually suggesting excess or a lack of restraint; sometimes neutral when describing eagerness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use greedily to describe eating, reading or grabbing things eagerly, often with disapproval. In a casual setting people more often say they ate it all up or wolfed it down. Greedily can sound a bit literary, so it is usually used in writing or a deliberate description.

distinctions.note: Eagerly is neutral or positive enthusiasm; greedily suggests selfish excess.
Hungrily describes appetite; greedily adds a sense of wanting more than one should.

examples.everyday: The kids grabbed the cookies greedily before anyone else could reach the plate.
examples.professional: The investors greedily pursued short-term returns and ignored the long-term risks in the market.
examples.analytical: The narrator describes the miser who counts his coins greedily, revealing a character defined by an insatiable desire for possessions.

nuance.analogy: Greedily is like a child reaching for the last slice of cake before anyone else can take it.
nuance.etymology: From greedy, from Old English graedig, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as a full sound; it is a reduced schwa, so say GREE-duh-lee.
Confusing greedily with greedy in position: greedily modifies a verb, while greedy modifies a noun.

greedily.etymology: From Middle English *gredyly*, *gredily*, from Old English *grǣdiglīce*, *grǣdelīce*; equivalent to *greedy* + *ly*.

senses.definition: In AI: Tying a model's answers to real sources or data, so they can be checked.

The interconnecting metal chassis or frame of a device, appliance, machine, or metal raceway via a designated conductor to earth at the service panel. It may be bare or covered, and does not carry current in normal operation.
senses.example: Before replacing the outlet, the electrician checked the grounding wire connected to the metal panel.

senses.definition: The act by which a child is grounded (forbidden from going out, using electronics, etc.).
senses.example: Because he missed curfew, his parents gave him a week of grounding without his phone.

senses.definition: Fundamental knowledge or background in a field or discipline.
senses.example: Her strong grounding in statistics made the transition into machine learning feel natural.

senses.definition: The return to a fully conscious state after a psychedelic experience.
senses.example: After the trip ended, the grounding took nearly an hour, during which he sat quietly on the couch.

senses.definition: The collision of a ship with ground beneath the surface of the water.
senses.example: The tanker suffered serious hull damage in a grounding off the rocky coast last winter.

senses.definition: The prevention of aircraft takeoff because of government action.
senses.example: The grounding of all flights to the island lasted three days after the government order.

senses.definition: The absorption of energy through visualized roots descending from oneself into the ground, using chi.
senses.example: During the qigong session, the instructor led us through grounding to draw energy from the earth.

senses.definition: The background of embroidery, etc.
senses.example: She filled the grounding with tiny white stitches so the blue flowers would stand out.

core.definition: In AI, the process of linking a model's answers to real sources or data so they can be checked.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending -ing is a short, reduced vowel followed by ng, not a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is positive in AI discussions because it means the answers can be verified.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use grounding in AI and machine learning to describe connecting a model's output to documents, databases or images. In everyday speech, grounding can mean a calming technique, or the electrical connection to earth in homes and buildings. For a child being punished, Americans say grounded.

distinctions.note: Retrieval is finding relevant documents, while grounding is making the answer rely on and cite them.
Verification is checking a result, while grounding is the step that connects the output to sources that make checking possible.

examples.everyday: The chatbot now shows which web pages it used, which is a kind of grounding.
examples.professional: Our next release will add better grounding so support agents can trace every answer to a policy.
examples.analytical: Grounding is often treated as a technical fix, but it also raises questions about what counts as evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a student writing footnotes that point to the books behind each claim.
nuance.etymology: From ground, from Old English grund, meaning base or bottom.
common_mistakes: Using grounding for the electrical sense when talking about AI, or the reverse without context.
Pronouncing the ending as a long ee sound.

conversation.text: Grounding means tying each answer to specific sources the model was given, ideally with citations.
Without grounding, the assistant answers from memory, and that's where most of the errors come from.
In vision-language models, grounding can also mean linking a phrase to a region of the image.
The electrician said the outlet lacked proper grounding.

senses.definition: Adult, physically mature.
Of, pertaining to, or suitable for adults.
senses.example: The museum has a grown-up exhibit about war that children should not see.

senses.definition: Having a mature outlook.
senses.example: Despite his age, he was surprisingly grown-up about the breakup.

senses.definition: An adult.
senses.example: If you see an injustice being done, do the right thing: tell a grown-up about it.

core.definition: Adj: adult, physically mature, and no longer a child. Noun: an adult person, often used when talking to or about children.

pronunciation.tip: When used before a noun, the first part is stressed, so say GROHN-up, not grohn-UP. Keep the final vowel short and relaxed (uh), and do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing maturity, but it can sound scolding when used as a command, as in 'Be a grown-up about it.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'grown-up' in casual speech, especially with children or about family matters, and 'adult' in formal or legal contexts. Saying 'Be a grown-up' to an adult can sound condescending, so use it with care. A common natural reply to someone who tells you to act your age is simply to agree or to apologize.

distinctions.note: 'Adult' is more formal and neutral, and is used in legal, medical and official language, while 'grown-up' is conversational and often emphasizes behaving maturely.
'Mature' describes emotional or intellectual development in a general way, while 'grown-up' is more casual and common in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: Honestly, you need to act like a grown-up and just call your sister back.
examples.professional: We need a grown-up conversation about why the launch slipped, not more finger-pointing in the meeting.
examples.analytical: In this tradition, moral responsibility is a grown-up virtue that requires accepting the consequences of one's own choices.

nuance.analogy: Like a house that has finished being built: it is no longer under construction, and it is expected to hold its own weight.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'grown', the past participle of 'grow', and 'up'.
common_mistakes: Using 'grown-up' as a plural noun without the hyphen or s in the right place: write 'grown-ups' for the plural noun.
Stressing the second word (grohn-UP) when used before a noun; the first word normally carries the stress.

senses.definition: A person, company, or organization that provides a guarantee.
senses.example: The bank asked her brother to serve as guarantor on the apartment lease.

core.definition: A person or organization that promises to pay or perform if another party fails to do so.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, TOR, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. The first vowel is the short e of 'bed', and the -ee- sound is not used. Keep the r rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and legal; it describes a responsibility rather than a quality of character.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use guarantor mainly in finance, law, and real estate, such as a cosigner on a loan or lease. In everyday talk, Americans say 'cosigner' for a loan or lease, and 'guarantee' or 'backer' for a promise. A natural reply in a lease context is 'Yes, my parent signed as the guarantor.'

distinctions.note: Guarantee can be a promise or a person who gives one; guarantor refers specifically to the person or entity taking on the obligation.
Cosigner is the common everyday term for a person who signs a loan with you; guarantor is more formal and sometimes implies a secondary obligation.

examples.everyday: My aunt was the guarantor on my apartment lease, so the landlord called her when I was late.
examples.professional: The bank requires a guarantor for any business loan above fifty thousand dollars.
examples.analytical: In contract theory, the guarantor's liability is secondary, attaching only when the primary debtor defaults.

nuance.analogy: Like a safety net under a trapeze artist: it catches the fall only if the performer slips.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French garantour, from garantir, to guarantee.
common_mistakes: Confusing guarantor with guarantee when a person is meant.
Saying GAR-an-ter with a stressed first syllable instead of stressing TOR.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, Hebrews 7:22 says Jesus has become the surety of a better covenant. The Greek word is engyos, a guarantee or pledge, and the passage presents Christ as the one who secures God's promise. Key passages: Hebrews 7:22, which calls Jesus the surety of the new covenant; Genesis 43:9, where Judah offers to be a pledge for Benjamin; and Proverbs 6:1-5, which warns against standing surety for a stranger's debt.

senses.definition: Someone who guards, watches over, or protects.
senses.example: The guardian of the historic church keeps the keys and opens it each morning.

senses.definition: A person legally responsible for a minor (in loco parentis).
A person legally responsible for an incompetent person.
A superior in a Franciscan monastery.
senses.example: The guardian of the friary assigned the brothers their duties for the week.

senses.definition: A major or final enemy; boss.
senses.example: Level twelve's final guardian is a giant stone dragon that guards the ancient crystal.

senses.definition: A servicemember of the United States Space Force.
senses.example: The guardian assigned to the satellite program reviewed the launch schedule with engineers.

core.definition: A person who protects or cares for someone, especially a child whose parents cannot care for them, or who is legally responsible for them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GAR, with the r clearly pronounced. The middle syllable is a quick 'dee' and the ending is a light 'un', not 'ian' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies care, protection, and responsibility, though the legal sense can sound formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use guardian for a child's legal caretaker, on school and medical forms, and in the phrase guardian angel, which is often said playfully about someone who helps you. For a neighbor who only watches your house, caretaker or babysitter is more natural. In a legal setting, Americans say legal guardian.

distinctions.note: A guard is usually a job protecting a place, while a guardian has legal responsibility for a person.
A parent is a biological or adoptive mother or father, while a guardian is appointed by law and need not be a relative.
A custodian often means someone who looks after a building or physical care, while a guardian implies legal responsibility.

examples.everyday: My sister is the kids' guardian if something happens to my husband and me.
examples.professional: The school needs the legal guardian's signature on the field trip form before Friday.
examples.analytical: The guardian is charged with the child's welfare, which makes the role ethical as well as legal.

nuance.analogy: Like a lifeguard at a pool, a guardian watches closely so the person in their care stays safe.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French guardein, from garder, meaning to watch over.
common_mistakes: Using guardian for a security guard, which is a different job in American English.
Stressing the last syllable as gar-dee-AN instead of GAR-dee-un.
nuance.biblical_note: In Galatians 4:2 RSV, an heir is under guardians and trustees until the date set by the father; the Greek epitropos means a steward or guardian appointed by a father. In 1 Peter 2:25 RSV calls Christ the Shepherd and Guardian of souls, where the Greek episkopos, usually overseer, is rendered as guardian.

guardian.etymology: From Middle English *gardein*, *garden*, from Old French *guardein*, from the verb *guarder*, of origin.

senses.definition: The quality of being hackneyed.

core.definition: The state of being overused and stale, so that an idea, phrase, or work no longer seems original or interesting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ed' in hackneyed is pronounced like a short 'id', not 'ed', and the final '-ness' ends in a weak schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies that something has lost its freshness through overuse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use the noun 'hackneyedness' in conversation. They usually say 'hackneyed' or 'a cliché' instead. The noun appears in book reviews, critiques, and academic writing when a critic wants to name the quality of overuse.

distinctions.note: A cliché is a specific overused phrase or idea, while 'hackneyedness' names the general quality of being stale.
'Triteness' stresses dullness and lack of depth; 'hackneyedness' stresses overuse and loss of freshness.
'Banality' refers to ordinariness or obviousness; 'hackneyedness' refers to a worn-out quality from repetition.

examples.professional: The pitch deck's hackneyedness made it hard to remember anything distinctive about the product.
examples.analytical: The hackneyedness of the sermon's imagery blunted its force for a congregation that had heard it all before.

nuance.analogy: Like a song played so often on the radio that you stop hearing it.
nuance.etymology: From hackneyed, from hackney, a horse for hire that was used so often it became commonplace.
common_mistakes: Using 'hackneyedness' in casual speech, where 'cliché' or 'hackneyed' is more natural
Stressing the final syllable instead of the first

senses.definition: A long forward pass with little chance of completion, typically used by the losing team when time is running out and no other play is practical, in a desperate attempt to score the winning points.
senses.example: Down by four with two seconds left, the quarterback threw a Hail Mary pass into the end zone.

senses.definition: An act done in desperation, with only a very small chance of success.
senses.example: Asking the bank for a loan with no collateral was our Hail Mary pass.

core.definition: A long, desperate forward pass in American football, thrown at the end of a half or game with little chance of catching it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls mainly on pass, with Mary carrying secondary stress. Pronounce Mary as 'MAIR-ee,' like the word merry, not as 'MAR-ee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive in sports, and desperate in tone. It can suggest courage in a long-shot situation or a lack of better options.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mainly for American football, especially at the end of a half or game. It is also used figuratively for any last-minute, long-shot attempt at success. The name echoes the Catholic prayer Hail Mary, but in sports talk it has no religious meaning; a common reply in conversation is 'Did it work?' or 'Is that a real chance?'
word_family: hail mary (adjective, informal, as in a hail mary attempt)

distinctions.note: The prayer is a Catholic and Orthodox devotion to Mary, while the football term is a sports phrase with no religious meaning.
A long pass is any forward throw over a distance, while a Hail Mary is a desperate, low-probability throw at the end of a game.

collocations: the Hail Mary at the buzzer

examples.everyday: We were down by four with two seconds left, so the quarterback threw a Hail Mary and somebody actually caught it.
examples.professional: The launch is in twelve hours and we still have a critical bug, so this patch is a Hail Mary fix that we hope holds.
examples.analytical: Calling a desperate last attempt a Hail Mary reveals how sports language shapes the way people describe long-shot risk.

nuance.analogy: A Hail Mary pass is like a long-shot lottery ticket: it is thrown with hope, not with a plan you can rely on.
nuance.etymology: Named after the Catholic prayer Hail Mary, which begins with the greeting words of the angel to Mary; the football sense dates from American sports slang.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing Mary as 'MAR-ee,' which sounds unnatural in American speech.
Using Hail Mary only for religious prayer, when in American English the phrase is much more often used for football or a last-minute attempt.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase's religious source is the Hail Mary prayer, which draws on Luke 1:28, where the angel Gabriel greets Mary, and Luke 1:42, where Elizabeth blesses her. The Greek word chaire, meaning rejoice or greetings, lies behind the opening word hail, and the football phrase itself is not a biblical term.

hail-mary-pass.etymology: From *Hail Mary*, a prayer for intercession, plus *pass* (“moving the ball from one player to another”).

senses.definition: Synonym of trichotillomania.
senses.example: Her therapist said her hair-pulling disorder had worsened during finals week.

core.definition: A mental health condition in which a person repeatedly pulls out their own hair, causing noticeable hair loss and distress.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on HAIR in the compound and on OR in disorder. Say 'pull' with a short u as in 'full', and keep the r in both 'hair' and 'disorder'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and clinical. The term describes a recognized condition, so it is used with sensitivity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in clinical, counseling, or academic settings. The DSM-5 lists it as trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder), and many people say 'trich' or 'pulling' in support groups. In everyday talk, people often say 'I have a pulling problem' or 'a hair-pulling habit' rather than the full clinical name.

distinctions.note: Trichotillomania is the older medical name for the same condition, and the DSM-5 uses both names; hair-pulling disorder is the more descriptive English term.
Excoriation disorder, or skin-picking disorder, involves repeatedly picking at skin rather than pulling hair, though both are body-focused repetitive behaviors.

collocations: habit reversal training for hair-pulling disorder

examples.everyday: My cousin has hair-pulling disorder and is working with a therapist, so please be patient with her.
examples.professional: Our counseling center runs a support group for clients who have hair-pulling disorder.
examples.analytical: Hair-pulling disorder appears in DSM-5 among the body-focused repetitive behaviors, which the authors distinguish from obsessive-compulsive disorder.

nuance.analogy: Like nail biting, a habit that becomes compulsive, but it leaves visible marks on the scalp.
nuance.etymology: Trichotillomania comes from Greek thrix (hair), tillein (to pull), and mania; the English name hair-pulling disorder is descriptive.
common_mistakes: Confusing hair-pulling disorder with alopecia areata, which is an autoimmune cause of hair loss rather than a self-directed behavior.
Stressing the wrong syllable in trichotillomania; the main stress falls on -MAY- in the middle of the word.

senses.definition: A large basket, usually with a cover, used for the packing and carrying of articles or small animals.
senses.example: a hamper of wine

senses.definition: A wicker or plastic basket specifically for holding laundry (from clothes hamper).
senses.example: I tossed my dirty jeans into the hamper before heading out to the gym.

senses.definition: A shackle; a fetter; anything which impedes.
senses.example: His heavy debts were a hamper that kept him from accepting the new job offer.

senses.definition: Articles ordinarily indispensable, but in the way at certain times.
senses.example: Hikers often find heavy packs a hamper when scrambling over steep, rocky ridges.

senses.definition: To put into a hamper.
senses.example: Competition pigeons are hampered for the truck trip to the point of release where the race back starts.

senses.definition: To put a hamper or fetter on; to shackle.
senses.example: The guards hampered the prisoner with heavy irons before marching him to the courtyard.

senses.definition: To impede in motion or progress.
senses.example: Heavy snow hampered rescue crews as they searched for the missing hikers overnight.

core.definition: A large basket, usually with a lid, used for carrying food, clothes, or other items, or a basket for dirty laundry.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HAM. The second syllable ends in a rhotic r sound, so the word ends in a soft er. Do not say ham-PAR.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an ordinary household or picnic word.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, a hamper usually means a laundry hamper in a bedroom or bathroom. For a food basket, Americans often say a picnic basket. As a verb, hamper means to hinder, and it is common in news and business writing.

distinctions.note: Basket is the general word. Hamper usually suggests a larger container, often with a lid or for laundry.
Hinder is the general word for slowing something down. Hamper often suggests making progress harder in a way that is noticeable.

collocations: put the clothes in the hamper

examples.everyday: Could you put your dirty shirts in the hamper instead of leaving them on the floor?
examples.professional: The new approval process has hampered the team's ability to ship updates on schedule.
examples.analytical: Poor documentation can hamper a research project because it makes results hard to reproduce and verify.

nuance.analogy: A hamper is a container for holding things together until someone carries them away, like a sack that gathers what needs to be moved.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English hanper, an alteration of hanaper, a basket.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as ham-PER.
Using hamper to mean a food basket in ordinary American speech, where picnic basket is more natural.
Confusing the verb hamper with hammer, which is a tool.

hamper.etymology: From Middle English *hamper*, contracted from *hanaper*, *hanypere*, from Anglo-Norman *hanaper*, Old French *hanapier*, *hanepier* (“case for holding a large goblet or cup”), from *hanap* (“goblet, drinking cup”), from **hnapp* (“cup, bowl, basin”), from…

senses.definition: One who harangues.
senses.example: The street-corner haranguer shouted about corporate greed until the lunch crowd had mostly drifted away.

core.definition: A person who gives a long, angry, forceful speech or lecture to others, often in a way that wears people down.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RANG, and the final -gue of 'harangue' is silent. The last syllable is a reduced 'er' sound, not a full 'ayr'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests someone who lectures or scolds others at length and does not listen.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'haranguer' in everyday speech. You will see it in essays, political commentary and literary writing. In casual talk people say 'ranter' or 'lecturer' for a similar meaning.

distinctions.note: An orator is a skilled public speaker who is admired, while a haranguer is a noisy, forceful speaker who is often resented.
A demagogue appeals to popular prejudice to gain power, while a haranguer is defined mainly by the lengthy, angry manner of speaking.

examples.professional: The meeting became a stage for one haranguer who lectured the team for forty minutes about deadlines.
examples.analytical: The essayist presents the public intellectual not as a haranguer but as a patient interlocutor who invites disagreement.

nuance.analogy: Like a foghorn that keeps blasting long after everyone has heard the warning.
nuance.etymology: From 'harangue', from Italian 'aringa', meaning a public speech, with the agent suffix '-er'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -gue as a hard g sound, when it is silent.
Confusing it with 'harasser', which refers to someone who bothers or threatens people.

core.definition: The name of a family head among the Israelites who returned from Babylonian exile with Ezra and Nehemiah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HASH. The final syllable is a reduced 'um' sound, not 'oom'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name used in biblical lists and scholarly discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Hashum in Bible study, church history, and academic work on Ezra and Nehemiah. It is not used in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Hasshub is a different name in Nehemiah, so keep them separate when reading the lists.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group found Hashum in the list of families who came back from Babylon.
examples.professional: The slide lists the returning families, including Hashum, with their numbers from Ezra 2.
examples.analytical: The inclusion of Hashum's family in the returnee lists shows the care taken to record ancestral identity after exile.

nuance.analogy: Hashum is like a name on a family roll call, a marker that identifies a household returning home.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ḥashum, a personal name, possibly meaning rich or having a fortune.
common_mistakes: Confusing Hashum with Hasshub, which is a different name.
Stressing the second syllable, saying 'ha-SHUM'.
nuance.biblical_note: Hashum (Hebrew Ḥashum) is the name of a family head whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile. Ezra 2:19 lists the sons of Hashum among the exiles who came back to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel. Nehemiah 7:22 gives the same family in a parallel list, and Ezra 10:33 names descendants of Hashum among those who had married foreign wives and were asked to separate from them. These lists show the importance of family identity in the post-exilic community.

senses.definition: An illness caused by overheating a person or animal beyond its body's capacity to regulate internal temperature.
senses.example: The marathon runner collapsed from heatstroke after running for hours in ninety-degree weather.

core.definition: A dangerous condition in which the body overheats and cannot cool itself, often causing confusion, fainting, or worse.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first word, HEAT, and the second part is a lighter secondary stress; say HEET-stroke with the final sound 'k' clearly. Non-native speakers often add an extra vowel between 't' and 's' or drop the 'k'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a serious medical emergency, and people use it with concern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use heatstroke in weather warnings, sports news, and medical advice, especially during summer heat waves. It is more serious than heat exhaustion and calls for calling 911 immediately. Americans also say 'heat stroke' in some writing, but the one-word spelling is standard.

distinctions.note: Heat exhaustion is a less severe condition with heavy sweating and weakness, while heatstroke involves a body temperature above about 104°F and confusion or loss of consciousness.
Sunstroke is an older term for heat illness caused by sun exposure; heatstroke is the current medical term and can happen indoors as well.

examples.everyday: If your dog stops responding and is panting hard in the car, it could be heatstroke, so get help right away.
examples.professional: The construction safety manager reminded the crew to drink water often because heatstroke is a serious risk on summer job sites.
examples.analytical: Heatstroke is best understood as a failure of thermoregulation, in which heat production and environmental heat overwhelm the body's capacity to dissipate it.

nuance.analogy: Heatstroke is like a car engine that overheats past the point where the cooling system can keep up, so damage starts to happen.
nuance.etymology: Heat is from Old English hǣtu; stroke comes from Old English strācian 'to stroke', and in this sense refers to a sudden blow or attack.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second word, as in heat-STROKE, which sounds unnatural in American speech.
Confusing heatstroke with heat exhaustion, which is much less dangerous.

conversation.text: Heatstroke is serious, so call 911 if someone gets confused or faints.
The coach stopped practice because he was worried about heatstroke.
Don't leave the dog in the car; it can get heatstroke in minutes.

senses.definition: Crowded with people.
Of the chest, rising and falling noticeably from exertion, emotion, or labored breathing.
Of the bosom, full, ample, or voluptuous in form, irrespective of movement.
senses.example: The portrait showed a woman with a heaving bosom and rosy cheeks.

senses.definition: An occasion on which something heaves or is heaved.
senses.example: The crew gave one final heaving on the rope and the anchor finally lifted.

core.definition: Rising and falling noticeably, usually from exertion or strong emotion, especially of the chest. Also, crowded with people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the vowel is long, as in 'heave' (rhymes with 'leave'). Do not use the short i of 'hive' or 'hiving'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on context. A heaving chest suggests strain, distress, or passion. A heaving crowd suggests discomfort or density.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'heaving' most often for a person's chest after running, crying, or lifting, and in the phrase 'heaving with people' for a crowded place. The noun sense, meaning an act of heaving, is rare in everyday speech. In descriptive writing it sounds vivid; in casual talk you might say 'out of breath' or 'packed'.

distinctions.note: Panting means breathing fast and in short, shallow gasps, often with the mouth open. Heaving describes a slower, deeper rise and fall of the chest.
'Crowded' is a neutral, general word for many people in one place. 'Heaving' with people is more vivid and suggests the place is full and moving.

examples.everyday: The subway platform was heaving with commuters at rush hour, so we waited for the next train.
examples.professional: After the outage, our support inbox was heaving with tickets, and the team stayed late to triage them.
examples.analytical: The poem's heaving chest imagery makes grief physical before it becomes abstract.

nuance.analogy: Like a sea swell lifting and dropping a boat, a heaving chest rises and falls with the body's effort.
nuance.etymology: From heave (Old English hebban, 'to lift').
common_mistakes: Saying the word with a short i like 'hiving', which is the sound of 'beehive'.
Confusing the adjective with the verb 'heave' in the past tense, which is 'heaved'.

senses.definition: Weekly, occurring once a week.

core.definition: Happening once a week, or lasting for a week; weekly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, DAH, and the ending is a reduced 'uh-dul'. Don't stress the first syllable or pronounce the 'b' as silent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, somewhat old-fashioned term for weekly events.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use hebdomadal in conversation; they say weekly instead. You might see it in academic, legal, or literary writing, or in historical descriptions of church or school schedules. Using it in everyday speech can sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: Weekly is the common everyday word, while hebdomadal is formal and literary.
Biweekly means every two weeks, while hebdomadal means once a week.

examples.everyday: Our weekly team lunch is the only hebdomadal ritual I look forward to.
examples.professional: The department holds a hebdomadal review of open tickets every Monday morning.
examples.analytical: The monastic community's hebdomadal rhythm of prayer structured the life of its members around the sabbath.

nuance.analogy: A hebdomadal event is like a weekly tide, returning on a regular seven-day cycle.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hebdomas, 'a group of seven' or 'week', from hebdomos, 'seventh'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as HEB-dom-uh-dul.
Using hebdomadal in casual speech where weekly is more natural.

senses.definition: Made or crafted by cutting, whittling down.
senses.example: The cabin's walls were built from hand-hewn logs cut by his great-grandfather.

senses.definition: Having been cut or mown down.
senses.example: The field lay bare, its wheat hewn down by the early autumn storm.

core.definition: Shaped or cut roughly from a larger piece, usually by chopping with an axe or similar tool.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long yoo sound, rhyming with tune and soon. Do not add a syllable such as hewn-ed.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it suggests rugged, handmade craftsmanship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hewn mostly for wood, stone and handcraft, such as hand-hewn beams or rough-hewn furniture, and in literary or real-estate writing. It is less common in speech than cut or carved. Rough-hewn is the most frequent form and is often used figuratively for someone unpolished but sincere.

distinctions.note: Carved implies detailed, deliberate shaping, while hewn suggests heavy, rough cutting.
Cut is neutral and everyday; hewn highlights chopping with an axe or adze and leaves a rough finish.

examples.everyday: The cabin has hand-hewn beams that someone must have cut by hand a century ago.
examples.professional: The renovation kept the original hewn timber frame and sanded only the surfaces guests actually touch.
examples.analytical: The poem's rough-hewn diction, deliberately unpolished, mirrors the hard lives of the farmers it describes.

nuance.analogy: Like a block of marble that a sculptor has chopped out but not yet smoothed.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hēawan, 'to cut', with the past participle hewn.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with two syllables or as hewed.
Using hewn as the simple past in everyday speech; hewed is the usual past tense, and hewn is the participle or adjective.
nuance.biblical_note: Hewn stone recurs in Scripture. In Amos 5:11 the prophet condemns those who build houses of hewn stone while oppressing the poor, using the Hebrew word gāzît for hewn stone. In Mark 15:46 Jesus is laid in a tomb hewn out of rock, where the Greek verb latomeō means to cut stone from a quarry.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to winter; brumal or hiemal.
senses.example: The hibernal stillness of the frozen farmland made the valley feel abandoned until March.

core.definition: Relating to winter, or characteristic of the winter season.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, BUR, which is a stressed r-colored vowel. The final syllable is a reduced schwa followed by l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly poetic. It is an elevated word for winter that suggests cold, stillness, or quiet.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use hibernal in conversation; it appears mainly in literary writing, nature writing, or formal description. In everyday speech, people say 'wintry' or 'winter'. Use it if you want a precise or elegant word in an essay or poem.

distinctions.note: Wintry is the common everyday word for cold, snowy weather; hibernal is rare and more literary.
Hibernate is a verb for animals sleeping through winter; hibernal is an adjective describing the season or its qualities.

examples.everyday: The house felt cold and quiet, with that hibernal stillness you get after a big snowstorm.
examples.professional: In the grant narrative, we described the field season as hibernal, because access roads close from December to March.
examples.analytical: The poet uses hibernal imagery to suggest a suspended time in which the speaker's grief seems frozen in place.

nuance.analogy: Hibernal is like a winter coat for the word winter: it says the same thing with a heavier, more formal fabric.
nuance.etymology: From Latin hibernalis, 'of winter', from hibernus, from hiems, 'winter'.
common_mistakes: Confusing hibernal with hibernate and using it as a verb.
Using hibernal in casual conversation, where wintry sounds more natural.

senses.definition: In a hideous manner.
To an extreme degree.

core.definition: To an extremely unpleasant or shocking degree; in a way that is very ugly or frightening.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HID. The middle syllables are quick and the last syllable is 'lee,' not 'lay.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something extremely ugly, shocking or unpleasant. Americans also use it loosely to mean 'extremely,' often in a playful or exaggerated way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hideously' to describe things that are truly ugly or frightening, such as 'a hideously expensive hotel' or 'a hideously loud party.' In casual speech it is a strong intensifier, so use it when you want to exaggerate. It is more common in writing and conversation than 'horribly,' but both are natural.

distinctions.note: 'Horribly' often describes an unpleasant experience or a bad result, while 'hideously' focuses more on ugliness or shocking appearance.
'Extremely' is neutral and can be used for anything. 'Hideously' carries a strong negative judgment, so it is not a good choice for something merely large or expensive without negative feeling.

examples.everyday: That couch was hideously expensive, so we just bought a cheap chair instead.
examples.professional: The first draft of the dashboard was hideously cluttered, so we removed half the charts before the review.
examples.analytical: Such a theory is hideously reductive, because it treats moral agency as a simple mechanical outcome.

nuance.analogy: Think of a fluorescent light that flickers in a dark room: it is so harsh and ugly that it draws all your attention for the wrong reasons.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'hideous' with the adverb ending '-ly.' 'Hideous' comes from Middle English 'hidous,' related to an older word meaning fear or horror.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllables too strongly, as in 'HID-ee-OUS-lee'; the main stress stays on the first syllable.
Using 'hideously' for mild things; it is strong, so 'hideously good' sounds odd in most contexts.

senses.definition: Physically elevated, extending above a base or average level:
senses.example: The balloon rose high in the sky. The wall was high. a high mountain

senses.definition: Very elevated; extending or being far above a base; tall; lofty.
senses.example: The balloon rose high in the sky. The wall was high. a high mountain

senses.definition: Relatively elevated; rising or raised above the average or normal level from which elevation is measured.
senses.example: The shelf is too high for me to reach without a stool.

senses.definition: Pertaining to (or, especially of a language: spoken in) an area which is at a greater elevation, for example more mountainous, than other regions.
senses.example: Many high villages in the region still speak languages that the lowlanders barely understand.

senses.definition: Having a specified elevation or height; tall.
senses.example: three feet high three Mount Everests high

senses.definition: Elevated in status, esteem, or prestige, or in importance or development; exalted in rank, station, or character.
senses.example: The oldest of the elves' royal family still conversed in High Elvish.

senses.definition: Most exalted; foremost.
senses.example: the high priest, the high officials of the court, the high altar

senses.definition: Of great importance and consequence: grave (if negative) or solemn (if positive).
senses.example: high crimes, the high festival of the sun

senses.definition: Consummate; advanced (e.g. in development) to the utmost extent or culmination, or possessing a quality in its supreme degree, at its zenith.
senses.example: high (i.e. intense) heat; high (i.e. full or quite) noon; high (i.e. rich or spicy) seasoning; high (i.e. complete) pleasure; high (i.e. deep or vivid) color; high (i.e. extensive, thorough) scholarship; high tide; high [tourism] season; the High Middle Ages

senses.definition: Advanced in complexity (and hence potentially abstract and/or difficult to comprehend).
senses.example: The lecture on Bayesian hierarchical models was far too high for most first-year students.

senses.definition: Extreme, excessive; now specifically very traditionalist and conservative.
senses.example: high church High Tory

senses.definition: Elevated in mood; marked by great merriment, excitement, etc.
senses.example: in high spirits

senses.definition: Keen, enthused.
senses.example: She was high on the idea of starting a community garden.

senses.definition: Intoxicated; under the influence of a mood-altering drug, formerly usually alcohol, but now (from the mid-20th century) usually not alcohol but rather marijuana, cocaine, heroin, etc.
senses.example: He was too high to drive, so he called a ride home.

senses.definition: Luxurious; rich.
senses.example: high living, the high life

senses.definition: Lofty, often to the point of arrogant, haughty, boastful, proud.
senses.example: a high tone

senses.definition: With tall waves.
senses.example: The surf was high at the point, so the lifeguards closed the beach.

senses.definition: Remote (to the north or south) from the equator; situated at (or constituting) a latitude which is expressed by a large number.
senses.example: high latitude, fish species in high arctic and antarctic areas

senses.definition: Large, great (in amount or quantity, value, force, energy, etc).
senses.example: My bank charges me a high interest rate.

senses.definition: Having a large or comparatively larger concentration of (a substance, which is often but not always linked by "in" when predicative).
senses.example: Carrots are high in vitamin A. made from a high-copper alloy

senses.definition: Acute or shrill in pitch, due to being of greater frequency, i.e. produced by more rapid vibrations (wave oscillations).
senses.example: The note was too high for her to sing.

senses.definition: Made with some part of the tongue positioned high in the mouth, relatively close to the palate.
senses.example: In phonetics, the vowel in beat is a high front vowel.

senses.definition: Greater in value than other cards, denominations, suits, etc.
senses.example: I have KT742 of the same suit. In other words, a K-high flush.

senses.definition: Having the highest rank in a straight, flush or straight flush.
senses.example: I have KT742 of the same suit. In other words, a K-high flush.

senses.definition: Winning; able to take a trick, win a round, etc.
senses.example: North's hand was high. East was in trouble.

senses.definition: Strong-scented; slightly tainted/spoiled; beginning to decompose.
senses.example: Epicures do not cook game before it is high.

senses.definition: Of a ball, above the batter's shoulders.
senses.example: the pitch (or: the ball) was high

senses.definition: Near, in its direction of travel, to the (direction of the) wind.
senses.example: The sailboat was sailing high, close to the wind, toward the harbor.

senses.definition: Positioned up the field, towards the opposing team's goal.
senses.example: Our defensive line is too high.

senses.definition: In or to an elevated position.
senses.example: How high above land did you fly?

senses.definition: In or at a great value.
senses.example: Costs have grown higher this year again.

senses.definition: At a pitch of great frequency.
senses.example: I certainly can't sing that high.

senses.definition: A high point or position, literally (as, an elevated place; a superior region; a height; the sky; heaven) or figuratively (as, a point of success or achievement; a time when things are at their best, greatest, most numerous, maximum, etc).
senses.example: It was one of the highs of his career.

senses.definition: The maximum atmospheric temperature recorded at a particular location, especially during one 24-hour period.
senses.example: Today's high was 32 °C.

senses.definition: A period of euphoria, from excitement or from an intake of drugs.
senses.example: That pill gave me a high for a few hours, before I had a comedown.

senses.definition: A drug that gives such a high.
senses.example: The users wanted a stronger high, so they tried the new pills.

senses.definition: A large area of elevated atmospheric pressure; an anticyclone.
senses.example: A large high is centered on the Azores.

senses.definition: The highest card dealt or drawn.
senses.example: Her high card was a king, which beat my pair of nines.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of high school.

core.definition: Extending far upward from a base or the ground; above the normal or average level in height, position, or amount.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable that rhymes with 'sky' and 'buy.' The 'gh' is silent, so don't add a sound for it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. It can be positive, as with high standards, or negative, as with high prices or high stress, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'high' constantly, for buildings, prices, temperatures, expectations and mood. Phrases such as 'high school,' 'high five' and 'high-speed internet' are everyday American expressions. For people's height, Americans usually say 'tall' rather than 'high.'

distinctions.note: 'Tall' is used mainly for people, trees and buildings that are narrow and upright. 'High' is used for position above a base, such as a high shelf or high ceiling.
'Lofty' is more formal or literary and suggests noble or grand ideals, as in lofty goals.

examples.everyday: The shelf is too high for the kids to reach, so I'll put the cereal up there.
examples.professional: Our error rate is still high, so we need to fix the data pipeline before the next release.
examples.analytical: The author argues that high expectations can sometimes undermine the moral seriousness of a community.

nuance.analogy: High is like the top shelf of a bookcase: it is above the normal line of reach, so you need extra effort or a ladder to get there.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'heah,' meaning elevated or lofty.
common_mistakes: Saying 'high' for a person's height, as in 'He is high'; Americans say 'He is tall.'
Pronouncing the 'gh' as a sound, as in 'hi-guh'; it is silent.

high.etymology: From Middle English *high*, *heigh*, *heih*, from Old English *hēah* (“high, tall, lofty, high-class, exalted, sublime, illustrious, important, proud, haughty, deep, right”), from **hauh* (“high”), from Proto-Germanic **hauhaz* (“high”), from…

senses.definition: The side of a hill.

core.definition: The sloping side of a hill, especially the part that is used for a house, farm, path or view.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a clear 'side' with a diphthong. Keep the 'l' clear and do not add a vowel between 'l' and 's'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hillside in everyday descriptions of land, houses, hiking and views, such as a house on a hillside. It is a plain, friendly word, and it is used both for natural slopes and for developed land.

distinctions.note: A slope is any inclined surface, while a hillside is specifically the side of a hill or mountain.
A hilltop is the top of a hill, whereas a hillside is the sloping part below it.

examples.everyday: We rented a little cabin on the hillside, and the view of the lake is amazing in the morning.
examples.professional: The crew will need a permit before they can clear trees on the hillside for the new access road.
examples.analytical: The erosion patterns on the hillside suggest that water runoff, rather than the original slope angle, drove the landslide.

nuance.analogy: Think of a hill as a roof: the hillside is the slanted part of the roof, not the peak.
nuance.etymology: Compound of hill and side, from Old English hyll and sīde.
common_mistakes: Confusing hillside with hilltop when describing location.
Pronouncing the word with a stressed second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture often describes hills and high places as sites of worship, and 1 Kings 14:23 says that Judah built high places and pillars on every high hill, which shows how hillsides were used for religious practice.

senses.definition: A collection containing a variety of miscellaneous things.
senses.example: His latest sculpture is a hodgepodge of kitchen clutter and scrap glued together.

senses.definition: A confused mass of ingredients shaken or mixed together in the same pot.
senses.example: The pantry shelves held a hodgepodge of canned beans, expired spices, and mismatched lids.

senses.definition: To move or position in an erratic, disorganized manner.
senses.example: They hodgepodged the boxes into the truck without any plan at all.

core.definition: A confused mixture of many different things, often without clear order or connection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is also pronounced with a clear 'ahj' sound, so it sounds like 'HAHJ-pahj'. Note the 'j' sound, not a 'd' followed by 'zh'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or humorous; it suggests disorder, though it can be affectionate for a homey mix.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hodgepodge for a messy collection of things, such as a closet full of random items or a menu with unrelated dishes. It is casual and works in both speech and writing. You can use it lightly about a hodgepodge of ideas or a hodgepodge of cultures.

distinctions.note: Mishmash is nearly synonymous and equally informal; hodgepodge is slightly more common in American speech.
An assortment is a deliberate, arranged selection, while a hodgepodge implies disorder.

examples.everyday: My garage is a hodgepodge of old bikes, paint cans, and holiday decorations.
examples.professional: The report was a hodgepodge of disconnected data sources, so we need to standardize the pipeline.
examples.analytical: The policy was less a coherent plan than a hodgepodge of compromises shaped by competing interest groups.

nuance.analogy: A hodgepodge is like a junk drawer: everything is useful somewhere, but nothing is arranged in a sensible order.
nuance.etymology: Originally a dish of mixed meats and vegetables, from the 1500s, from 'hotch-potch' with altered spelling.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a 'd' and 'zh' sound instead of a 'j' sound.
Using 'a hodgepodge' with plural nouns without thinking; it is singular, so say 'a hodgepodge of things'.

hodgepodge.etymology: From Middle English *hochepoche*, a variation of *hochepot*, from Old French *hochepot*, from Middle Dutch *hutspot* (“beef or mutton cut into small pieces and mixed and boiled together in a pot”), from *hotsen*, *hutsen* (“to shake; jog; jolt”) + *pot*…

senses.definition: Towards home.
senses.example: I am homeward bound.

senses.definition: Oriented towards home.
senses.example: I caught a homeward bus.

core.definition: In the direction of home; toward your home. As an adjective, it describes something moving or facing toward home.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HOHM. The ending -ward is pronounced as an r-colored 'wurd,' not with a broad 'ah' vowel like 'wahrd.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound warm or wistful depending on context, especially in phrases like 'homeward bound.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'homeward' mainly in writing, travel talk, and phrases like 'heading homeward' or 'homeward bound.' In everyday speech people more often say 'on the way home' or 'heading home.' 'Homewards' with an s is considered a British-leaning variant and is less common in American use.

distinctions.note: Homebound can mean traveling toward home or confined to home by illness, while homeward names only the direction of movement.
Homewards is a variant with the same meaning, but Americans usually prefer homeward.

examples.everyday: We stopped for gas and then headed homeward before the rain started.
examples.professional: The sales team finished the client visit and is flying homeward tomorrow morning.
examples.analytical: Odysseus's long struggle is, in many ways, a homeward journey that tests what home really means.

nuance.analogy: Like a compass needle swinging back to north, the homeward traveler's thoughts keep turning toward the same point.
nuance.etymology: Old English ham meaning home, plus -weard meaning turned toward.
common_mistakes: Using a preposition after 'homeward,' as in 'homeward to the house'; the word already carries the direction.
Saying 'homewards' as the default American form, when 'homeward' is more common.

homeward.etymology: From Middle English *homward*, from Old English *hāmweard*, from Proto-Germanic **haimawarda*, equivalent to *home* + *ward*.

senses.definition: A rod bent into a curved shape, typically with one end free and the other end secured to a rope or other attachment.
senses.example: Hang your coat on the hook behind the back door.

senses.definition: A barbed metal hook used for fishing; a fishhook.
senses.example: He baited the hook with a worm and cast the line into the lake.

senses.definition: Any of various hook-shaped agricultural implements such as a billhook.
senses.example: The farmhand used a hook to cut back brambles along the irrigation ditch.

senses.definition: The curved needle used in the art of crochet.
The part of a hinge which is fixed to a post, and on which a door or gate hangs and turns.
senses.example: The top hook on the gate had rusted, so the gate sagged toward the driveway.

senses.definition: A loop shaped like a hook under certain written letters, for example, g and j.
senses.example: In handwriting class, the teacher showed us how to form the hook on a lowercase g.

senses.definition: A tie-in to a current event or trend that makes a news story or editorial relevant and timely.
senses.example: Her editorial used the Super Bowl ad controversy as a hook to discuss corporate advertising.

senses.definition: A snare; a trap.
senses.example: The con artist baited his hook with promises of easy money.

senses.definition: An advantageous hold.
senses.example: The wrestler got a hook on his opponent's arm and wouldn't let go.

senses.definition: The projecting points of the thighbones of cattle; called also hook bones.
senses.example: The butcher pointed to the hook bones on the steer and explained how the cut was made.

senses.definition: Removal or expulsion from a group or activity.
senses.example: He is not handling this job, so we're giving him the hook.

senses.definition: A field sown two years in succession.
senses.example: The back forty is a hook this year, sown in barley two seasons in a row.

senses.definition: A grasp (of), an attachment (to).
A brief, punchy opening statement intended to get attention from an audience, reader, or viewer, and make them want to continue to listen to a speech, read a book, or watch a play.
senses.example: Her speech opened with a hook about a child who had never seen the ocean.

senses.definition: A gimmick or element of a creative work intended to be attention-grabbing for the audience; a compelling idea for a story that will be sure to attract people's attention.
senses.example: The producers liked the pitch, but they wanted a stronger hook for the pilot episode.

senses.definition: A finesse.
senses.example: Her hook with difficult clients made her the team's best negotiator.

senses.definition: A jack (the playing card).
senses.example: She led with the hook of spades, expecting her partner to win the trick.

senses.definition: A sharp bend or angle in the course or length of an object (e.g. a bend in a river, etc.).
senses.example: The river takes a sharp hook just past the old mill, so boats slow down there.

senses.definition: A spit or narrow cape of sand or gravel turned landward at the outer end, such as Sandy Hook in New Jersey.
senses.example: We walked out along the sandy hook at low tide to see the lighthouse.

senses.definition: Part of a system's operation that can be intercepted to change or augment its behavior.
senses.example: We've added hooks to allow undefined message types to be handled with custom code.

senses.definition: An instance of playing a word perpendicular to a word already on the board, adding a letter to the start or the end of the word to form a new word.
A diacritical mark shaped like the upper part of a question mark, as in ỏ.
Senses relating to sports. A curveball.
senses.example: He threw a hook in the dirt.

senses.definition: A basketball shot in which the offensive player, usually turned perpendicular to the basket, gently throws the ball with a sweeping motion of his arm in an upward arc with a follow-through which ends over his head. Also called hook shot.
A ball that is rolled in a curved line.
A type of punch delivered with the arm rigid and partially bent and the fist traveling nearly horizontally mesially along an arc.
senses.example: The heavyweight delivered a few powerful hooks that staggered his opponent.

senses.definition: A golf shot that (for the right-handed player) curves unintentionally to the left. (See draw, slice, fade.)
The amount of spin placed on a bowling ball.
A prostitute.
Synonym of shoulder (“the part of a wave that has not yet broken”).
A catchy musical phrase which forms the basis of a popular song.
senses.example: The song's hook snared me.

senses.definition: A ship's anchor.
A curveball.
senses.example: He threw a hook in the dirt.

senses.definition: A type of shot played by swinging the bat in a horizontal arc, hitting the ball high in the air to the leg side, often played to balls which bounce around head height.
(rare) A háček.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (historical) A knee-shaped wooden join connecting the keel to the stem (post forming the frontmost part of the bow) or the sternpost in cog-like vessels or similar vessels.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To attach a hook to.
senses.example: Hook the bag here, and the conveyor will carry it away.

senses.definition: To become attached, as by a hook.
senses.example: The utensil holder hooks onto the side of the dishrack.

senses.definition: To catch with a hook.
senses.example: He hooked a snake accidentally, and was so scared he dropped his rod into the water.

senses.definition: To work yarn into a fabric using a hook; to crochet.
To insert in a curved way reminiscent of a hook.
senses.example: He hooked his fingers through his belt loops.

senses.definition: To ensnare or obligate someone, as if with a hook.
senses.example: She's only here to try to hook a husband.

senses.definition: To steal.
To connect (hook into, hook together).
senses.example: If you hook your network cable into the jack, you'll be on the network.

senses.definition: To make addicted; to captivate.
senses.example: He had gotten hooked on cigarettes in his youth.

senses.definition: To acquire as a spouse.
To succeed in heeling the ball back out of a scrum (used particularly of the team's designated hooker).
To use the hockey stick to trip or block another player.
senses.example: The opposing team's forward hooked me, but the referee didn't see it, so no penalty.

senses.definition: To swerve a ball; kick or throw a ball so it swerves or bends.
To engage in prostitution.
senses.example: I had a cheap flat in the bad part of town, and I could watch the working girls hooking from my bedroom window.

senses.definition: To play a word perpendicular to another word by adding a single letter to the existing word.
To finesse.
To seize or pierce with the points of the horns, as cattle in attacking enemies; to gore.
To bend; to be curved.
To move or go with a sudden turn.
To play hooky; to skip school or a class.
senses.example: They hooked English, sneaking out behind the school and smoking cigarettes.

senses.definition: To play a hook shot.

core.definition: A curved piece of metal, plastic, or wood, attached to a surface, used to hang, catch, or fasten things.

pronunciation.tip: This is a one-syllable word with a short 'oo' sound, as in 'book,' not the long 'oo' of 'hook' in 'hoot.' Keep the final k crisp and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. The word can be positive in phrases like 'a hook for the coat' and negative when it means entrapment, as in 'the hook of addiction.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hook' constantly for everyday objects: a coat hook, a fishhook, a hook on a wall for keys. The phrasal verbs 'hook up' and 'hook on' are common in casual talk. In music, a 'hook' is the catchy part of a song, and in sports, 'hook' also names a curving shot or punch.

distinctions.note: A hanger is shaped to hold clothes, while a hook can hold anything and is usually fixed to a wall or ceiling.
A latch is a catch that keeps a door or gate closed, while a hook is used to hang or fasten an object.
A peg is a short, simple wooden or plastic pin for hanging things, often without a curve.

examples.everyday: Can you hang your jacket on the hook by the door so it doesn't end up on the floor?
examples.professional: The design team added a hook to the chart so that the key metric stands out in the dashboard.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that the moral hook of an argument often matters more than its logical structure in persuading listeners.

nuance.analogy: A hook is like a question mark on a wall, holding up whatever you need to keep off the floor.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'hōc,' a bent or angled object.
common_mistakes: Using 'hook' as a verb with the wrong preposition: 'hook it to the wall' is fine, but 'hook it at the wall' sounds wrong.
Confusing 'hook up' (connect, or start dating) with 'hook' (fasten with a hook), which can change the meaning in conversation.

hook.etymology: From Middle English *hoke*, from Old English *hōc* (“angle, point, hook”), from **hōk*, from Proto-Germanic **hōkaz*, variant of **hakô* (“hook”), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **kog-*, **keg-*, **keng-* (“peg, hook, claw”).

senses.definition: (historical) A member of a tribal group of antiquity who inhabited the region near Mount Seir, and possibly other areas of the Levant.
senses.example: The Bible describes the Horites as early inhabitants of Mount Seir before the Edomites arrived.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A member of an ancient people who lived in the hill country of Seir, southeast of the Dead Sea, according to the Hebrew Bible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the r is pronounced. The final syllable rhymes with 'kite', not with 'eat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical and scriptural term with no everyday emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in biblical studies, archaeology, or Bible teaching. It would not come up in ordinary conversation. Do not confuse it with Hittite, a different ancient people.

distinctions.note: Hittites were an Anatolian people with their own empire, while Horites were a separate group associated with Seir and the region later called Edom.
Edomites were descendants of Esau who settled in the same area, and Scripture says they displaced the Horites there.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group got into a discussion about the Horites, and nobody had heard of them before.
examples.professional: In the lesson on Edom, I summarized the Horites as the earlier inhabitants of Seir, before Esau's descendants arrived.
examples.analytical: The genealogy of Seir the Horite in Genesis 36 raises questions about how the biblical writers understood the relationship between Edom and earlier populations.

nuance.analogy: Like an old place name that survives on a map after the people who gave it have been absorbed or displaced, the Horites persist mainly as a name in the text.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew hōrî, an ethnic name whose origin is debated; some scholars connect it with the Hurrians.
common_mistakes: Confusing Horite with Hittite or Hurrian, which are different peoples
Adding an extra syllable, such as 'hor-EYE-tuh', instead of two syllables
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew hōrî (ḥōrî), a people name. Genesis 14:6 describes Chedorlaomer and his allies defeating the Horites in the hill country of Seir. Genesis 36:20 names Seir the Horite as an early inhabitant of the land, and the chapter lists his descendants, whose clans were later absorbed into Edom. Deuteronomy 2:12 says the Horites lived in Seir before the descendants of Esau drove them out and settled in their place.

senses.definition: The human race; mankind, humanity; Homo sapiens.

core.definition: The human race considered as a whole; all people on Earth, also called mankind or humanity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the last syllable, KIND, and the first syllable sounds like 'hyoo' with a y-glide. Do not reduce the middle syllable to nothing; say it as a quick 'muhn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it often appears in discussions of shared purpose, history or the future.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use humankind in speeches, essays and news writing when they want a gender-neutral alternative to mankind. In casual talk people usually say people or everyone instead. It is a mass noun, so you say 'humankind has' and not 'humankinds'.

distinctions.note: Humanity can mean the whole human race, but it also means compassion or kindness; humankind refers only to the species.
Mankind is the older term and many Americans now avoid it because it seems to exclude women; humankind is the neutral alternative.

examples.everyday: People have survived worse than this, so I think humankind will get through it.
examples.professional: Our climate report is meant to help policymakers plan for what humankind will face over the next fifty years.
examples.analytical: Theologians have long asked what distinguishes humankind from the rest of creation, and whether that difference is biological, moral or relational.

nuance.analogy: If the universe were a huge book, humankind would be the single chapter written by one species.
nuance.etymology: From human plus kind, with kind meaning a race or species, from Old English.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in HU-mankind; the main stress is on KIND.
Using humankinds as a plural; the word is uncountable.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'adam means man or humankind and is related to 'adamah, meaning ground. Genesis 1:27 describes God creating humankind in his image, male and female. Genesis 2:7 says the LORD God formed man of dust from the ground, linking humankind to the earth.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or having the form of a hypercube.

core.definition: Relating to a hypercube, a geometric figure in four or more dimensions, or having its structure.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on HY, with a secondary stress on KYOO. The vowel in the last syllable is short, like the 'i' in 'bit,' so avoid turning the ending into 'bik' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: This is a technical adjective used in mathematics, computer science, and physics. Ordinary Americans rarely use it, but it appears in textbooks and research papers on high-dimensional geometry or network design. When discussing it with non-specialists, say 'four-dimensional cube-like' instead.

distinctions.note: Cubic describes shapes in three dimensions, while hypercubic refers to the extension of a cube into four or more dimensions.
A tesseract is one specific four-dimensional hypercube, while hypercubic is the adjective describing that kind of structure.

examples.everyday: The science fiction movie showed a hypercubic spaceship, which was hard for me to picture.
examples.professional: We used a hypercubic lattice to model the neighbor structure in the simulation, which made the data easier to analyze.
examples.analytical: The hypercubic arrangement of the vertices makes the symmetry group easy to count, which is the key step in the proof.

nuance.analogy: A cube is a square extended into a third direction; a hypercube does the same thing once more, into a fourth direction.
nuance.etymology: From hyper-, meaning 'beyond,' and cubic, from Greek kybos, 'cube.'
common_mistakes: Confusing hypercubic with cubic, which means only three dimensions.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as hy-per-KYOO-bik.

senses.definition: Expressing doubt or skepticism.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see I,‎ think.

core.definition: Used to soften a statement, showing that it is your opinion and that you are not completely sure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THINK. Make the th voiceless with the tongue between the teeth, and let the final k be unreleased, not 'sink'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It softens statements and sounds polite, but too many uses can make you sound unsure, especially in formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I think' constantly to offer opinions: 'I think we should go.' It can come at the start or end of a sentence: 'That's good, I think.' In professional email, 'I believe' sounds more confident, but 'I think' is perfectly natural in meetings. The dictionary's figurative and idiomatic senses are not needed here.

distinctions.note: 'I believe' is more formal and suggests stronger conviction than 'I think'.
'I guess' is more casual and shows more uncertainty than 'I think'.
'I suppose' is mild and often resigned, and it sounds a bit more formal than 'I think'.

examples.everyday: This coffee is really good. I think I'll get another one.
examples.professional: I think we should move the review to Thursday so the data team has time to finish.
examples.analytical: I think the author's argument depends on an unstated assumption about independence, which the data never test.

nuance.analogy: Like a sticky note on your opinion, so people know it can be revised.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'I think' as a hedge with 'I think of,' which means having something in mind.
Overusing 'I think' in formal writing, which can make your argument sound tentative.

senses.definition: Saying you will send more information after the meeting.

core.definition: A phrase saying you will send more information or a summary in an email after a meeting or call.

pronunciation.tip: The verb follow is stressed on FAH, and up is the stressed particle of the phrasal verb in this phrase. The word by is reduced, and email stresses the second syllable, so it sounds like 'ih-MAYL'.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this at the end of meetings to show they will take responsibility for the next steps. The phrase is common in business email and sounds professional. A natural reply is 'Great, thanks, I'll look for it.'

distinctions.note: Simpler and less specific; follow up implies a continuation of an earlier conversation or task.

collocations: follow up on the action items

examples.everyday: Thanks for the advice about the car, I'll follow up by email if I need anything else.
examples.professional: Thanks for the discussion today, I'll follow up by email with the action items and owners.
examples.analytical: I'll follow up by email with the revised definitions, since the argument depends on how we describe the terms.

nuance.analogy: Like leaving a sticky note on the desk after a meeting to say what happens next.
common_mistakes: Saying 'follow up to email' instead of 'follow up by email'.
Forgetting the stress on up in the phrasal verb, which makes the phrase sound flat.

conversation.text: I don't have the numbers here, but I'll follow up by email.
Thanks for the questions. I'll follow up by email with the details.

senses.definition: Saying you're tired after a busy or difficult day.
senses.example: I've had a long day, so I'm ordering takeout and going straight to bed.

core.definition: Casual statement that you are tired because the day was busy, demanding or stressful.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DAY. Long has the ng sound at the end, not an added g; the vowel in 'had' is the short a of 'cat,' not the ah of 'father.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It signals tiredness and asks for sympathy or understanding without complaining.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this at the end of a workday, when they get home, or when they meet a friend after work. A natural reply is 'Oh no, what happened?' or 'Sit down and tell me about it.' It is friendly and safe in almost any setting.

distinctions.note: Exhausted is stronger and more physical; 'I've had a long day' gives a reason and is milder.
Rough means something bad or unpleasant happened; long only means the day was full.

collocations: a long day in the office

examples.everyday: Hey, I've had a long day, so I'm ordering pizza tonight.
