Calling someone an isolationist is a strong political charge, so it is usually said by critics. In casual talk people more often say he doesn't want to get involved or he's against sending foreign aid.

distinctions.note: Isolated describes a place or person cut off from others, while isolationist describes a political attitude toward other countries.
A nationalist emphasizes a nation's pride and interests; an isolationist specifically avoids foreign involvement, though the two views often overlap.
Non-interventionist is a more neutral, policy-focused term that many people prefer, because isolationist carries a pejorative tone.

examples.everyday: My uncle says we should stop sending money overseas, and honestly, that makes him a bit of an isolationist.
examples.professional: The senator's isolationist stance on trade worries our export partners, so we should prepare a response before the hearing.
examples.analytical: Isolationist arguments often rest on the premise that domestic security and foreign entanglement are fundamentally opposed, a premise that historians have challenged.

nuance.analogy: An isolationist country is like a house with the doors locked and the windows shut: safe from visitors, but cut off from the neighborhood.
nuance.etymology: From isolation plus -ist; isolation comes from Italian isolato, from Latin insula, island.
common_mistakes: Confusing isolationist (a political view) with isolated (lonely or cut off), as in saying I am isolationist when you mean you feel alone.
Using it for any shy or private person; it refers only to a national stance on foreign affairs.
Pronouncing the final syllable as -est instead of a short -ist.

senses.definition: One who issues, emits, or publishes.
senses.example: The bond issuer must disclose its financial statements to investors every quarter.

core.definition: A company, bank, government, or other organization that offers or puts out securities, cards, or money for public use.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -er is an r-colored vowel, not 'ar'. Keep the middle syllable 'shoo' light and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise business or legal term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use issuer mainly in finance, banking, and law, as in 'card issuer' or 'bond issuer'. In daily life people say 'my bank' or 'the company' instead. In business writing, issuer names the organization that puts out the security or card.

distinctions.note: A publisher makes books, magazines or digital content, while an issuer releases financial instruments or cards.
A lender provides a loan, while an issuer offers securities or cards that may come with or without a loan.

examples.everyday: My credit card issuer sent me a new card after the data breach.
examples.professional: We need the issuer's approval before we can list the bonds on the exchange.
examples.analytical: Whether the issuer or the investor bears the risk of default is the central question in this contract.

nuance.analogy: An issuer is like a mint: it creates the coin, and everyone else holds it once it is out in circulation.
nuance.etymology: From issue plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'oo' followed by 'ar', instead of an r-colored 'er'.
Using issuer for a person who sells things, when it refers to an organization that releases securities or cards.
Confusing issuer with issuance, which is the act of issuing rather than the party doing it.

senses.definition: A method capable of performing the same action on every item in a collection.
senses.example: The Python loop calls the iterator once per element until the collection is exhausted.

senses.definition: One who or that which iterates.
senses.example: She was a relentless iterator, revising each prototype dozens of times before the team approved it.

core.definition: An object or method that moves through the items of a collection one at a time, returning each in turn.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable strongly, with a lighter stress on the -ray part; the final -or is a reduced er sound. Learners often say it-uh-RAY-tor with a full vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no social weight.
nuance.usage_note: Programmers and data scientists use iterator mainly in languages such as Python and Java. Non-programmers rarely use it. The second sense, one who iterates, is rare and generic. In code you often call iter() or let a for loop create one for you.

distinctions.note: An iterable is the collection you can loop over; an iterator is the object that keeps track of your place as you move through it.
A generator is a kind of iterator created by a function that yields values one at a time, often without storing them all.

examples.everyday: My friend who codes said the app uses an iterator to load each photo only as you scroll down.
examples.professional: I wrote a custom iterator so the pipeline reads the log files one line at a time without loading them all into memory.
examples.analytical: An iterator separates the act of traversal from the structure being traversed, which is why one loop can serve many different collections.

nuance.analogy: Like a bookmark: it remembers where you stopped and moves you to the next page.
nuance.etymology: From iterate plus the agent suffix -or; ultimately from Latin iterare, to repeat.
common_mistakes: Confusing an iterator with an iterable; a list is iterable, and you must get an iterator from it before calling next.
Pronouncing the final syllable with a strong or as in 'IT-uh-RAY-tore'; American speech uses a reduced er.

senses.definition: Any of several woody, climbing, or trailing evergreen plants of the genus Hedera.
senses.example: Dense English ivy covered the brick walls of the old library.

senses.definition: Any similar plant of any genus.
senses.example: The hikers learned to recognize poison ivy before wandering into the woods.

core.definition: A climbing or trailing evergreen vine, especially English ivy, that clings to walls, fences, and tree trunks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -y is a tense 'ee' sound, so it is not 'eye-vuh' or 'ih-vee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in gardening and architecture, since it suggests greenery and age. It can be negative when the vine damages walls or is hard to remove.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ivy for the climbing plant on brick buildings, garden walls, and yards, and they often talk about pulling ivy off a fence. Poison ivy is a different plant that causes a rash, so it is not a true ivy. Ivy League refers to eight prestigious northeastern universities, which is a separate, capitalized use.

distinctions.note: Vine is a general word for any climbing or trailing plant, while ivy names a specific plant group, often evergreen.
Virginia creeper is a related climbing plant that turns red in fall, and it is not a true ivy even though it looks similar.

examples.everyday: Pull that ivy off the fence before it takes over the whole backyard.
examples.professional: Facilities approved removing the ivy from the brick wall before the building inspection next week.
examples.analytical: Ivy clinging to old brick has become a literary emblem of a university's endurance and its slow, tenacious history.

nuance.analogy: Like a clingy friend who holds tight to a wall and keeps growing over everything.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ifig.
common_mistakes: Saying 'eye-vuh' with a short final vowel
Calling poison ivy a true ivy, which it is not

ivy.etymology: From Middle English *ivi*, from Old English *īfiġ*, from **ibig*, **ibag*, **ibah*, from Proto-Germanic **ibahs* (compare, *Ieloof*, ), from Proto-Indo-European **ebʰ*.

senses.definition: Any of several large North American hares of the genus Lepus.
senses.example: At dusk, a jackrabbit bolted across the highway in front of our headlights.

senses.definition: To make a sudden, rapid movement.
senses.example: When the fire alarm rang, the students jackrabbited out of the classroom toward the exits.

core.definition: A large, long-eared North American hare with long legs, known for its speed and found mostly in the West.

pronunciation.tip: Stress JACK and give a weaker secondary stress to RAB. The final -bit reduces to a soft schwa, so it sounds like 'rab-uht', not 'rabbit' with a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an animal, but 'jackrabbit start' can describe a car that accelerates fast.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'jackrabbit' for the large western hare, especially in deserts and open plains. Many people in the East just say 'rabbit' for the smaller cottontail. The phrase 'jackrabbit start' is common in car talk and sports, meaning a very fast start.

distinctions.note: Rabbits are usually smaller, with shorter ears, and most are born blind and naked in burrows, while jackrabbits are born furred with open eyes.
A cottontail is a small rabbit that Americans usually mean when they say 'rabbit' in a backyard, and it is not a jackrabbit.

examples.everyday: A jackrabbit darted across the highway in front of us, and I had to brake hard.
examples.professional: The wildlife survey counted jackrabbits along the transect near the reservoir.
examples.analytical: Ecologists study the jackrabbit as a prey species whose population cycles shape the food web of the desert.

nuance.analogy: A jackrabbit is like a runner with long legs built for sudden bursts of speed across open ground.
nuance.etymology: Named for its large ears, which resemble those of a jackass; 'jack' here refers to a male donkey, and 'rabbit' is the animal name.
common_mistakes: Calling the jackrabbit a 'rabbit' in formal writing when a zoologist would say 'hare'.
Stressing the second syllable of 'jackrabbit'.

senses.definition: A carnivorous spotted large cat native to South and Central America, Panthera onca.

core.definition: A large spotted cat of Central and South America with a heavy build and rosette markings, Panthera onca.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The w glides straight into the vowel, so it is one word, JAG-wahr, with a clear r at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the animal is often admired in nature talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use jaguar in zoos, nature shows, and conservation news. Many people also know Jaguar as a British car brand, so say the cat or the animal when you mean the wild animal. Wild jaguars live mainly in Mexico and South America, and only occasionally wander into southern Arizona.
word_family: jaguarundi (noun, a smaller wild cat of the Americas)

distinctions.note: Leopards live in Africa and Asia and are smaller; jaguars live in the Americas, have heavier builds, and often have a dot inside their rosettes.
A cougar, or mountain lion, is a plain tawny cat with no spots; a jaguar is spotted and heavier.

examples.everyday: We saw a jaguar at the zoo, and the kids couldn't stop staring at it.
examples.professional: Our conservation team tracks jaguar movement through the Amazon using camera traps.
examples.analytical: The jaguar's rosettes, some with central dots, are one of the features biologists use to identify individual animals.

nuance.analogy: Think of the jaguar as the heavyweight spotted cat of the Americas, where the leopard is its lighter cousin across the ocean.
nuance.etymology: From Tupi yaguara, a word for a wild beast.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (jag-WAR); the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Saying Jaguar alone when speaking about the animal, which can be confused with the car brand; add the cat or the animal to be clear.

related: jaguarundi (noun, a smaller wild cat of the Americas)

core.definition: A son of Simeon, one of the twelve tribal ancestors of Israel, and the founder of the Jaminite clan.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'JAY-min' rather than 'juh-MEEN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Jamin is a proper name used only in biblical and genealogical contexts. Americans may know it from Scripture or from the given name, which is uncommon in the United States.

examples.everyday: My friend named her new baby Jamin after a character in the Bible.
examples.professional: In the seminary lecture, the professor listed Jamin among the sons of Simeon in Genesis 46:10.
examples.analytical: The genealogical lists of Simeon, including Jamin, show how the tribe was organized by clan in the Pentateuch.

nuance.analogy: Like a name on a family tree, Jamin marks one branch of the tribe of Simeon.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yamin, meaning 'right hand' or 'south'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as in 'juh-MEEN'.
Confusing Jamin with Jamnia, a city.
nuance.biblical_note: Jamin is a son of Simeon listed among the sons who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:10) and in the later census lists (Numbers 26:12). Exodus 6:15 also names him among the sons of Simeon. He is the eponymous ancestor of the Jaminites.

senses.definition: Joking.
senses.example: Between the jesting and the pranks, the camp counselors barely got the kids to bed.

senses.definition: Bantering; ridicule.
senses.example: His constant jesting about my accent got old fast during the team dinner.

senses.definition: Mocking.
senses.example: Her jesting at the new hire's clumsy presentation embarrassed the whole department.

senses.definition: Facetious.
senses.example: He gave a jesting reply that made the serious committee members frown.

senses.definition: Humorous.
senses.example: The jesting tone of the wedding toast had everyone laughing until they cried.

senses.definition: Playful; mocking.
Jeering.
senses.example: A jesting crowd of fans heckled the referee after the disputed call.

core.definition: Said or done as a joke rather than seriously; playful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, keep the vowel short as in 'best,' and do not turn the -ing into 'een.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, but it can turn mocking depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say joking in everyday speech and use jesting mainly in writing, storytelling or formal speech. It can sound old-fashioned in casual conversation, where 'I'm just kidding' or 'I'm just joking' is natural. As a noun it means teasing or banter, and it becomes a put-down when the tone turns mocking.

distinctions.note: Joking is everyday and general; jesting sounds more literary and can imply a bit of teasing.
Teasing is playful and often affectionate, aimed at a person; jesting is more about the speaker's light tone or remark.
Mocking is contemptuous and meant to belittle; jesting is meant lightly, though it can slide into mockery.

examples.everyday: Half jesting, she told me the printer had a personal grudge against her.
examples.professional: His jesting comment about the deadline landed badly with the client, who heard it as a threat.
examples.analytical: The jesting tone of the satire masks a serious critique of the court's corruption.

nuance.analogy: A jesting remark is a pebble tossed into a pond: light on the surface, but it still makes ripples.
nuance.etymology: From jest, from Anglo-French geste, a deed or tale, from Latin gesta, deeds.
common_mistakes: Using jesting as a stiff everyday synonym for joking
Stressing the second syllable as jes-TING instead of JES-ting

senses.definition: In a joking manner.

core.definition: In a playful way, not seriously; as a joke.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ly is a clear 'lee' sound, and the middle syllable is short and reduced, so do not say 'JOH-keeng-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it softens a remark and signals that it is not meant seriously.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use jokingly to signal that a comment is not serious, as in 'He jokingly asked for a raise.' It is common in both speech and writing. It often appears with verbs like said, asked, or suggested. Saying something half jokingly means it is partly a joke.

distinctions.note: Playfully suggests lively fun in behavior, while jokingly focuses on the words being meant as a joke.
Seriously means in earnest; jokingly means not in earnest, so the two are opposites.

examples.everyday: When I asked if I could borrow his truck again, he jokingly said I should buy my own.
examples.professional: Our director jokingly suggested that we ship on a Friday, but she was not really serious about it.
examples.analytical: Locke jokingly describes the philosopher's thought experiment, yet it shapes his argument about the nature of personal identity.

nuance.analogy: Saying something jokingly is like wrapping a gift in bright paper: the content is still there, but the presentation makes it lighter.
nuance.etymology: From joking plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'jokingly' where 'playfully' is more natural for physical or lively behavior.
Placing it awkwardly in the sentence; it usually goes before the verb, as in 'He jokingly said'.
Mispronouncing the middle as 'JOH-keeng', with a long vowel.

senses.definition: A short period of time, typically anywhere from several seconds to several minutes or more.
senses.example: Give me just a minute to finish this email, and I'll be right with you.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see just,‎ a,‎ minute.
Stop; wait; hold on. Used to interrupt speech or proceedings so that one can make a comment or query.
senses.example: Just a minute! You can't change the password without confirming it first.

core.definition: Wait; hold on. Said to ask someone for a short pause before you continue speaking or acting.

pronunciation.tip: In fast speech, just and a are reduced to juhst and uh, and the stress falls on MIN in minute, pronounced MIN-it, not my-NOOT. Link the words so it sounds like juhst-uh-MIN-it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is polite when relaxed, but said sharply it can sound impatient or dismissive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Just a minute' or 'Hold on a sec' to pause a conversation, for example when someone is looking for a document or a phone rings. 'Just a moment' sounds more polite and is common in customer service. A natural reply is 'Sure, take your time' or 'No problem'. Literally, the phrase does not always mean sixty seconds; it often means a short unspecified wait.
word_family: minute (adjective, pronounced my-NOOT, meaning very small)

distinctions.note: Just a moment sounds slightly more polite and is common in customer service, while just a minute is more casual.
Hold on is very informal and can also mean keep holding a phone or an object, while just a minute is a clear request to wait.

examples.everyday: Just a minute, I'm still looking for my keys.
examples.professional: Just a minute, Dana, I want to check the figures before I agree.
examples.analytical: Just a minute: before we accept that claim, we should define what counts as evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like raising a hand in a meeting to pause the discussion until you are ready to speak.
nuance.etymology: Minute comes from Medieval Latin pars minuta prima, meaning first small part, which gave the time unit its name.
common_mistakes: Dropping the article, as in 'I'll be there in just minute' instead of 'in just a minute'.
Pronouncing minute as my-NOOT, which is the adjective meaning very small, instead of MIN-it for the time unit.

senses.definition: Relating to or characteristic of kakistocracy; governed by the worst.
senses.example: Columnists warned that the city council had grown kakistocratic under its newest, least competent members.

core.definition: Governed by the least qualified or most corrupt people; describing rule by the worst.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KRAT, the fourth syllable, and the ending '-ic' is a short 'ik' sound. Do not stress the -tuh- syllable or lengthen the ending.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It is a strong criticism of a government or leadership, and it suggests that the people in charge are unfit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective in op-eds, political analysis and essays when they want to attack a government's competence. It is rarely used in everyday talk, where people prefer phrases like 'totally incompetent' or 'a mess.' Using it casually can sound pretentious, so keep it for serious written or spoken critique.

distinctions.note: Incompetent describes a person or group lacking skill in general, while kakistocratic describes a whole system of rule by the worst.
Corrupt refers to dishonesty or bribery, whereas kakistocratic is about incompetence, though corruption is often implied.

examples.professional: The memo argues that our hiring freeze has created a kakistocratic culture in which managers keep only those who never challenge them.
examples.analytical: Her essay defines a kakistocratic regime as one in which institutional offices are filled by those least qualified to exercise them.

nuance.analogy: A kakistocratic government is like a ship steered by whoever volunteers, not by the navigator who knows the stars.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kakistos, 'worst', the superlative of kakos, 'bad', plus -kratia, 'rule'.
common_mistakes: Using it for ordinary incompetence in a small group; it is best reserved for governments or leadership systems.
Stressing the syllable -tuh- instead of KRAT.

senses.definition: To watch and pay attention to, in case of misbehavior or mishap.
senses.example: I must keep an eye on this sauce in case it curdles.

core.definition: To watch someone or something carefully to make sure nothing bad happens or goes wrong.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'eye,' and the 'an' and the 'on' are weak. Americans say 'an' as 'un' and often shorten 'on' to 'un'; do not give 'an' a strong 'am' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually suggests caring supervision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in everyday life to ask someone to watch a child, a pet, a bag, or the stove. A natural reply is 'Sure, I've got it' or 'Will do.' It is friendly and common, but in formal writing use 'monitor' or 'supervise.'

distinctions.note: Watch is the general verb for looking, while keep an eye on adds the sense of supervising or guarding against trouble.
Monitor is more formal and technical, often used for systems, data, or health, while keep an eye on is informal.

collocations: keep an eye on the kids
keep an eye on the oven
keep an eye on the stock price
keep an eye on the weather

examples.everyday: Could you keep an eye on my bag while I grab a coffee? Thanks, I'll be right back.
examples.professional: I'll keep an eye on the error rate after the deployment and send an update if anything spikes.
examples.analytical: A good teacher keeps an eye on the students who seem quiet, since silence can hide confusion as well as understanding.

nuance.analogy: Keeping an eye on something is like leaving a porch light on: you are not doing the work, but you are watching over it.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'on' and saying 'keep an eye' alone when the object is needed.
Saying 'keep eye on' without the article 'an.'

conversation.text: Can you keep an eye on my bag while I grab a coffee?
Let's keep an eye on the error rate after the release.
Keep an eye on the kids while I start dinner.

senses.definition: To hold back; to refuse to give or share.
To stay back; to refrain from approaching.
To restrict or restrain.
To prevent (a pupil) from advancing in a course.

core.definition: To stay at a distance from something, or to hold something back from someone instead of giving or revealing it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress usually lands on BACK, the particle, as in most phrasal verbs. The vowel in back is the short a of cat, not the long a of bake, and the final k is unreleased in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; keep back a crowd is neutral, but keep back information can sound secretive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say it for crowds ('Please keep back from the edge'), for holding back money or information ('They kept back some details from the report'), and sometimes for restraining yourself ('I kept back my anger'). It is common in news reports and police language. In casual talk many people would say hold back or stay back instead.

distinctions.note: Hold back is more common in everyday talk for restraining emotion or information, while keep back often sounds like staying at a distance or keeping something away.
Stay back is intransitive, meaning you remain at a distance yourself, while keep back can take an object, as in keep back the crowd.
Hold off means to delay an action, not to restrain people or withhold information.

examples.everyday: The officer asked everyone to keep back from the curb while the bus pulled in.
examples.professional: Please keep back a copy of the draft until legal signs off on the language.
examples.analytical: The narrator keeps back key facts until the final chapter, forcing readers to reconsider their earlier judgments.

nuance.analogy: Like a dam that holds water back from a valley, keep back holds people or information from moving forward.
nuance.etymology: Keep comes from Old English cēpan; back comes from Old English bæc.
common_mistakes: Using keep back for emotions; hold back tears is the more natural phrase.
Saying keep back to for moving away; the usual preposition is keep back from.

senses.definition: To maintain position; to prevent oneself from falling behind; to stay even or ahead of another while walking, driving, etc.
senses.example: They ran so fast I could hardly keep up.

senses.definition: To continue with (work, etc).
senses.example: Keep up the good work, team!

senses.definition: To ensure that one remains well-informed about something.
senses.example: I always try to keep up with (or "keep up on") current affairs.

senses.definition: To maintain; to preserve; to prevent from deteriorating or falling.
senses.example: Regular maintenance helps keep up the old bridge so it does not crumble.

senses.definition: To prevent someone from going to bed or to sleep.
senses.example: The crying baby kept me up all night

core.definition: To move or work at the same pace as others, or to stay informed about something that is changing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on UP. The vowel in "up" is the short "uh" sound, not "oo"; the final "p" is released lightly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans say "keep up" when walking with a group, when a job is demanding, or when following news in a field. It can be encouraging ("Keep up the good work") or mildly stressful ("I can't keep up with my email"). A natural reply is "Yeah, I'm trying to keep up."

distinctions.note: Catch up means to reach the same level after falling behind; keep up means to avoid falling behind in the first place.
Keep on means continuing an action; keep up means maintaining pace or staying informed relative to others or a standard.

examples.everyday: Slow down a little, I can't keep up with you on this hill.
examples.professional: I'm struggling to keep up with the changes in the reporting dashboard.
examples.analytical: Scholars must keep up with new empirical findings, or their theories soon fall out of step with the evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like running alongside a friend on a track: you stay close enough to remain in the same race.
common_mistakes: Omitting "with" in "keep up with someone or something."
Confusing "keep up" with "catch up" when describing someone who is already behind.

keep-up.etymology: From Middle English *kepen up* (“to perpetuate, maintain, preserve”), equivalent to *keep* + *up*.

conversation.text: Slow down, I can't keep up with you!
Great job, keep up the good work.
I try to keep up with the news, but it's exhausting.
It's hard to keep the house up when we're both working.

senses.definition: A set of keys laid out in a gridlike pattern, used for typing on a typewriter, computer, etc.
senses.example: I spent the afternoon retyping notes because my laptop keyboard kept sticking on the letter e.

senses.definition: A component of many instruments, including the piano, organ, and harpsichord, consisting of usually black and white keys that cause different tones to be produced when struck.
senses.example: The pianist ran her fingers across the keyboard, testing each ivory key before the concert.

senses.definition: An electronic device containing a keyboard (preceding sense), especially one that is capable of producing musical sounds when the keys are played.
senses.example: For his first band practice, he bought a cheap keyboard that could imitate a church organ.

senses.definition: To type on a computer keyboard.
senses.example: Keyboarding is the part of this job I hate the most.

core.definition: A panel of keys that you press with your fingers to type into a computer; also the row of keys on a piano or organ.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KEY. The second syllable is a strong, rhotic 'bawrd' with a clear r, and it does not have a separate 'oh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use keyboard for the typing device on a computer or phone and for the keys on a piano or synthesizer. The word is almost always a noun, and people say 'type' rather than using keyboard as a verb. Phrases like 'keyboard shortcut' and 'wireless keyboard' are everyday American terms.

distinctions.note: A keypad is a small set of number keys, such as on a phone or alarm, while a keyboard has the full set of letters.
A typewriter is a mechanical machine, while a keyboard is the part you press on a computer or instrument.
A piano is an instrument, while a keyboard can also mean an electronic instrument with keys.

examples.everyday: My old keyboard keeps sticking, so I finally bought a wireless one for my desk.
examples.professional: Please send feedback on the new keyboard layout by Friday so the design team can finalize it.
examples.analytical: Early typewriter keyboards shaped how writers thought about text, because the arrangement of keys constrained what could easily be typed.

nuance.analogy: A keyboard works like a bank of switches, with each key sending one specific signal to the machine.
nuance.etymology: From key plus board; board comes from Old English bord, a flat piece of wood.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'bord' with a long O or as two syllables.
Using keyboard for a single key; say 'press the Enter key' rather than 'press the Enter keyboard'.
Confusing keyboard with keypad when speaking about a phone or card reader.

core.definition: A town in Moab, named in Numbers, Jeremiah and Ezekiel; its name means two cities in Hebrew.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on THAY, the third syllable. Keep the middle syllables light and the final syllable short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical place name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Kiriathaim mostly in Bible study, sermons and academic work on the Old Testament. Speakers do not need it in everyday talk. When you mention it, people will recognize it as a town in Moab.

distinctions.note: Kiriath is the general word for city used in place names, while Kiriathaim is a specific town in Moab.

examples.everyday: During our Bible study, someone asked about Kiriathaim, and I said it was a town in Moab.
examples.professional: In my sermon prep notes, I wrote that Kiriathaim appears in the oracles against Moab in Jeremiah.
examples.analytical: Scholars link Kiriathaim to the Moabite cities condemned in Jeremiah 48, reading its name as a reference to a double settlement.

nuance.etymology: Hebrew qiryatayim, meaning two cities, from qiryah, city, in the dual form.
common_mistakes: Mixing Kiriathaim up with Kiriath-jearim, which is in Judah, not Moab.
Stressing the first syllable, as in KIR-ee-uh-thime.
nuance.biblical_note: Kiriathaim is a town in Moab, taken by the Reubenites in the time of Moses and later condemned by the prophets. Numbers 32:37 says the Reubenites rebuilt Kiriathaim, Jeremiah 48:1 and 48:23 place it among the cities judged against Moab, and Ezekiel 25:9 lists it among the Moabite towns. Its Hebrew name means two cities, which suggests a double settlement.

senses.definition: A continuous association of wage-earners for the purpose of maintaining or improving the conditions of their employment; a trade union.
senses.example: My uncle has worked at the steel plant for thirty years and belongs to the labor union.

core.definition: An organized association of workers that bargains collectively with employers over pay, benefits, and working conditions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of union, which sounds like 'YOON.' The second syllable is a light 'yun,' and the -or in labor is reduced, so avoid making it a full 'bor' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most settings. Members and supporters often see it positively, while critics may use it as a negative term when talking about costs or work rules.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say labor union or simply union, and both are everyday words. Trade union is mainly British, so Americans would not normally use it. People say things like 'She joined the union' or 'He's in the teachers' union,' with no 'the' needed before a trade.

distinctions.note: Trade union is the common British term, and Americans would say labor union or union instead.
A guild is a historical or craft association, and the term survives in names like the Screen Actors Guild. A labor union is the modern, workplace-bargaining organization.
Association is a general term for any group. Labor union specifically means workers who bargain with employers.

examples.everyday: My dad was a machinist for thirty years and never missed a union meeting.
examples.professional: The labor union agreed to a three-year contract that includes a modest raise and a new safety policy.
examples.analytical: In its classic form, the labor union turned scattered individual grievances into collective bargaining power.

nuance.analogy: A labor union is like a carpool that negotiates the price of gas for everyone instead of each driver bargaining alone.
nuance.etymology: Union comes from Latin unio, unity; labor comes from Latin labor, toil.
common_mistakes: Saying trade union, which sounds British in the US.
Using union alone for a university student union or the Union in Civil War history without context.
Saying in the union when the natural phrase is in a union or join the union.

senses.definition: Lagging behind; taking more time than the others in a group.
senses.example: The laggard team finished the data migration two days after everyone else.

senses.definition: (animal husbandry) Not growing as quickly as the rest of the flock or herd.
senses.example: The laggard broilers are euthanized and incinerated.

senses.definition: One who lags behind; one who takes more time than is necessary or more than the others in a group.
senses.example: Our manager gently reminded the laggard on the team that the quarterly report was due Friday.

core.definition: A person or thing that falls behind others, especially someone slow to act or make progress.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced 'er' sound, so say it quickly as 'erd' rather than 'ard.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests someone who is slow or behind and who should be doing better.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use laggard in news, business writing and formal speech about companies, countries or states that are slow to adopt something. It sounds somewhat old-fashioned in casual talk, so most people would say 'slowpoke' or 'behind the curve' in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: A straggler is someone who falls behind a group on a walk or march; laggard can describe any slowness in progress, not just physical lag.
Slowpoke is informal and often teasing; laggard is more formal and critical.

examples.everyday: Our team is a bit of a laggard when it comes to updating software, so we're always last to try new tools.
examples.professional: Our company is a laggard in cloud migration, so we need a roadmap to catch up with our competitors.
examples.analytical: Economists often classify countries as leaders or laggards based on how quickly they adopt new technologies.

nuance.analogy: A laggard is like the last runner in a race who never quite catches up to the pack.
nuance.etymology: From lag (verb) plus the suffix -ard, meaning one who habitually does something.
common_mistakes: Using laggard only for people; it can describe companies, countries or industries.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'ard' as in 'hard.'

senses.definition: An artistic representation of this event.
senses.example: The art history professor projected Leonardo's Last Supper onto the screen during our lecture.

core.definition: The final meal Jesus shared with his twelve apostles before his arrest and crucifixion, as described in the Gospels; also a famous painting of it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SUP in supper, and the second syllable is a reduced r-colored schwa, not 'per' or 'pair'. Avoid saying it like super, which has a long u.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to reverent. In religious settings it is solemn, but in art or pop culture it can be used casually or humorously.
nuance.usage_note: Americans capitalize Last Supper when referring to the biblical meal or Leonardo da Vinci's painting in Milan. In churches, Protestants often say Lord's Supper and Catholics say Eucharist or Mass for the same rite. Lowercase last supper can mean a final meal before a departure or closure, but it may sound dramatic. A natural reply to a 'Last Supper' joke is simply a laugh or 'Good one.'

distinctions.note: Lord's Supper is the common Protestant term for the rite of Communion, while Last Supper refers to the historical meal and the painting.
Dinner is the normal American word for the main meal, while supper is less common and can mean a lighter or informal evening meal.

examples.everyday: Have you seen the Last Supper painting in Milan? It is smaller than people expect.
examples.professional: The museum's education team wants a slide on the Last Supper for the Renaissance art course.
examples.analytical: The Synoptic Gospels and John place the Last Supper differently in relation to the Passover, a difference scholars still debate.

nuance.analogy: Like a famous family photo of a final dinner that everyone remembers and retells.
nuance.etymology: Supper from Old French soper, 'a light evening meal'; last from Old English.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing supper like super, which changes the vowel and the meaning.
Writing last super or lowercase last supper for the biblical meal and painting, when capitals are standard.
Assuming Catholics and Protestants use the same term; Catholics usually say Eucharist, while many Protestants say Lord's Supper.
nuance.biblical_note: The Last Supper is the meal Jesus shared with his disciples before his crucifixion. The Greek word deipnon (the main evening meal) appears in the Gospel accounts, and the meal is linked to the institution of the Lord's Supper.

traditions.view: The Last Supper is the origin of the Eucharist, which Catholics believe becomes the body and blood of Christ at consecration, a change called transubstantiation.
The Orthodox see the Last Supper as the origin of the Eucharist celebrated in the Divine Liturgy, in which Christ is really present, though they avoid precise philosophical definitions of how.
Lutherans affirm Christ's real presence in, with and under the bread and wine, while Reformed churches teach a spiritual presence and many Baptists and evangelicals see the meal as a memorial.

senses.definition: Near the end of a period of time.
senses.example: The seedlings appeared to be coming along nicely until a late frost killed them.

senses.definition: Specifically, near the end of the day.
senses.example: It was getting late and I was tired.

senses.definition: Associated with the end of a period.
senses.example: Late Latin is less fully inflected than Classical Latin.

senses.definition: Not arriving or occurring until after an expected time.
senses.example: The flowers were late in blooming because of the prolonged cold weather.

senses.definition: Levied as a surcharge on a payment which has not arrived by a specified deadline.
senses.example: The power company suspended late fees during the pandemic.

senses.definition: Not having had an expected menstrual period.
senses.example: I'm late, honey. Could you buy a test?

senses.definition: Recently deceased, dead: used particularly when speaking of the dead person's actions while alive.
senses.example: Her late husband had left her well provided for.

senses.definition: Recent — relative to the noun it modifies.
senses.example: the late war

senses.definition: Of a star or class of stars, cooler than the sun.
senses.example: Our astronomy project showed that the red dwarf is a late-type star, cooler than the sun.

senses.definition: (dated) Existing or holding some position not long ago, but not now; departed, or gone out of office.
senses.example: the late bishop of London
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: A shift (scheduled work period) that takes place late in the day or at night.
senses.example: I took a late on Thursday because the warehouse was short-staffed.

senses.definition: After a deadline has passed, past a designated time.
senses.example: We drove as fast as we could, but we still arrived late.

senses.definition: Formerly, especially in the context of service in a military unit.
senses.example: Colonel Easterwood, late of the 34th Carbines, was a guest at the dinner party.

senses.definition: Not long ago; just now, recently.
senses.example: The server has been acting up of late, so we restarted it twice.

core.definition: Happening or arriving after the usual, scheduled, or expected time.

pronunciation.tip: This word rhymes with 'eight' and 'gate'. Keep the diphthong smooth and don't add an extra vowel before the final t. In American speech the final t is often a clean, unreleased stop.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general, but negative when it describes a person who is not on time, because it suggests a lack of respect or a problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use late in everyday speech almost constantly, for arriving at work, meetings, parties, and appointments. The phrase 'Sorry I'm late' is the standard apology, and 'Don't be late' is a common instruction. For late night hours or things happening near the end of a period, Americans use late in the same way.

distinctions.note: Tardy is formal and used for official records, such as school or workplace attendance; late is the everyday word.
Delayed describes something scheduled that was postponed by an outside cause, such as a flight or a shipment; late can describe a person or an event that started after the planned time.
Behind means you are later than planned in a process or schedule; late means you are not present or not finished at the scheduled time.

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, the traffic on the freeway was awful.
examples.professional: Sorry I'm late to the sync; the data pull ran longer than expected.
examples.analytical: The reform arrived late, after the institutions had already hardened their positions.

nuance.analogy: Like a bus that pulls up to the stop after the posted time, leaving the waiting passengers stranded.
nuance.etymology: From Old English læt, slow or tardy, from a Germanic root meaning slow or behind.
common_mistakes: Writing 'I am late from work' instead of 'I am late for work'.
Confusing late with lately: 'I haven't seen you lately' is correct, but 'I haven't seen you late' is not.

late.etymology: From Middle English *late*, *lat*, from Old English *læt* (“slow; slack, lax, negligent; late”), from **lat*, from Proto-Germanic **lataz* (“slow, lazy”).

senses.definition: Tolerance of other people's views, particularly in religious context.
senses.example: Her church's latitudinarianism welcomed members who disagreed on nearly every doctrine.

senses.definition: The latitudinarian position, that de re attitudes are merely a special case of de dicto attitudes.
senses.example: Debates over de re and de dicto attitudes in the philosophy seminar eventually turned toward latitudinarianism.

core.definition: Religious tolerance: the view that a church or believer should accept a wide range of beliefs and practices instead of insisting on strict doctrinal agreement.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on NAIR, in the fourth syllable of a long word. Keep the 'ar' as a clear r sound, and make the final -ism as 'iz-um' with a weak vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in historical or scholarly contexts; it can sound positive to supporters of broad tolerance and negative to critics who see it as doctrinal laxity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in church history, theology, and academic discussions of Anglican history. It is rarely used in everyday conversation, where people say 'open-minded' or 'broad-minded' instead. The second sense in your list, about de re and de dicto attitudes, is a rare philosophy-of-language term, so the religious meaning is the one most learners will meet.

distinctions.note: Pluralism means accepting that many different groups and views coexist; latitudinarianism is a more specific religious attitude of accepting differences within one church.
Ecumenism is the active movement toward unity among different churches; latitudinarianism is more about the tolerance of doctrinal differences inside a church.

examples.professional: Our seminary's latitudinarianism means we teach several traditions side by side without ranking them, which our students appreciate.
examples.analytical: Eighteenth-century Anglican latitudinarianism tried to make reason and moral duty, rather than contested doctrine, the center of Christian belief.

nuance.analogy: It is like a big tent that welcomes many kinds of believers, while a fence keeps out anyone who does not match every doctrine exactly.
nuance.etymology: From latitudinarian, from Latin latitudo meaning breadth, with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with latitude in the geographic sense.
Using latitudinarian as an everyday adjective for open-minded people, which sounds overly technical.

senses.definition: The act of lauding; high praise or commendation.

core.definition: A formal expression of high praise, often given in a speech, tribute, or written commendation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, DAY. The ending -tion is pronounced "shun," not "tee-on."

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Laudation is a formal word used in literary criticism, ceremonies, obituaries and academic writing. Americans rarely use it in casual conversation, where praise or tribute is more natural. It can sound grand or slightly old-fashioned, so use it for formal occasions.

distinctions.note: Praise is the everyday word, while laudation is a formal noun for a speech or statement of high praise.
A tribute is an honor or statement of respect, often given at a memorial or event, while laudation is specifically the act of praising.

examples.everyday: At the retirement party, everyone gave the same kind of short laudation for her thirty years at the store.
examples.professional: The vice president delivered a short laudation for the engineers who shipped the platform.
examples.analytical: The essay reads less as analysis than as a laudation of the author's life, and so it avoids her more uncomfortable decisions.

nuance.analogy: A laudation is like a formal toast at a banquet, where the guest of honor is praised in front of everyone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin laudatio, from laudare, to praise.
common_mistakes: Using laudation for casual compliments, where praise would be more natural.
Confusing it with laudatory, which is an adjective, not a noun.

senses.definition: One who or that which launches. A device that throws something or the person who initiates a launch.
senses.example: The catapult made a good launcher for the small projectile.

senses.definition: An application that launches another or others, often holding icons or menus for frequently used programs.
senses.example: I installed a launcher on my laptop so my favorite apps appear in one tidy menu.

core.definition: A device that sends something into flight, or a software program that starts other applications.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAUNCH, and the -er is a weak r-colored syllable. The ch should be clear, not a sh sound, and the t is not pronounced separately.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a technical term without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, launcher appears mainly in technical or military contexts, such as rocket launcher or grenade launcher, and in computing, where an app launcher opens programs from a menu. Everyday speakers rarely use the word casually, so in conversation people usually name the object instead. In tech talk, app launcher or desktop launcher is clear to colleagues.

distinctions.note: A launch pad is the platform from which a rocket takes off, while a launcher is the device or system that sends the object or starts the program.
A dispenser releases small amounts of something repeatedly, while a launcher sends a single object or program forward with force.

examples.everyday: My dog loves the tennis ball launcher, so I use it every evening in the park.
examples.professional: Please pin the app launcher to the taskbar so the team can open the dashboard in one click.
examples.analytical: In Newtonian mechanics, a launcher is a source of initial conditions, and its precision determines the projectile's path.

nuance.analogy: A launcher is like a slingshot: it gives the object its initial push, and then the object carries itself.
nuance.etymology: From launch plus the suffix -er, one who or that which launches.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the t in launcher, making it LAWN-tcher; the ch sound should be clear.
Using launcher to mean the start of something, as in 'the launcher of the project'; say the launch of the project.

senses.definition: To incline, deviate, or bend, from a vertical position; to be in a position thus inclining or deviating.
senses.example: a leaning column

senses.definition: To incline in opinion or desire; to conform in conduct; often with to, toward, etc.
senses.example: I’m leaning towards voting Conservative in the next election.

senses.definition: To rest or rely, for support, comfort, to use as a hard surface for writing, etc.
senses.example: Grandpa likes to lean on his cane when he waits in line.

senses.definition: To hang outwards.
senses.example: The passengers leaned out the windows to watch the parade pass by.

senses.definition: To press against.
To thin out (a fuel-air mixture): to reduce the fuel flow into the mixture so that there is more air or oxygen.
senses.example: The mechanic had to lean the carburetor so the engine would stop running rich.

senses.definition: An inclination away from the vertical.
senses.example: The trees had various leans toward gaps in the canopy.

senses.definition: Meat with no fat on it.
senses.example: The butcher trimmed off every bit of fat and sold me the lean.

senses.definition: A recreational drug composed of codeine-promethazine cough syrup mixed with usually soda and associated with the hip-hop culture of the Southern United States.
senses.example: Doctors warned the teens that mixing lean with alcohol could cause fatal breathing problems.

senses.definition: An organism that is lean in stature.
senses.example: The thin greyhound was a lean that could outrun any dog in the county.

senses.definition: Slim; not fleshy.
senses.example: After months of training, he looked lean and strong for the championship fight.

senses.definition: Having little fat.
senses.example: lean steak cuts

senses.definition: Having little extra or little to spare; scanty; meagre.
senses.example: a lean budget

senses.definition: Having a low proportion or concentration of a desired substance or ingredient.
senses.example: A lean ore hardly worth mining.

senses.definition: Efficient, economic, frugal, agile, slimmed-down; pertaining to the modern industrial principles of "lean manufacturing".
senses.example: lean management

core.definition: To tilt or bend your body or an object away from vertical, or to rest your weight against something for support.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the only syllable, and the vowel is long, like the 'ee' in 'clean,' not the short 'i' in 'in.' Keep the final n clear, and don't say 'lane.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The verb is physical and descriptive. Its meaning shifts only when it's followed by 'to' or 'toward' for opinions, or when it describes body shape as an adjective.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'lean forward' to someone in a meeting, 'lean back' in a chair, or 'lean against the wall' in casual talk. Used with 'on,' it means depending on someone, as in 'lean on a friend.' Overuse in a formal report would sound informal, so use 'incline' or 'tilt' there.

distinctions.note: Tilt usually describes a small angle movement of an object, while lean often involves the body and a support.
Lean on is a phrasal verb meaning to depend on someone for help or emotional support, and it is less physical than lean alone.

examples.everyday: Can you lean back so I can see the screen?
examples.professional: In the meeting, the manager leaned forward and asked the team for the latest numbers.
examples.analytical: The argument leans on an assumption about human motivation that the author never defends.

nuance.analogy: Like a tree in a strong wind, the body leans away from straight up to keep its balance.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hlīnian, to lean or incline.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'lane' or 'lin' with a short vowel.
Confusing the verb lean with the adjective lean (slim) when speaking, since they share spelling and sound.

lean.etymology: From Middle English *lenen* (“to lean”), from Old English *hleonian*, *hlinian* (“to lean, recline, lie down, rest”), from **hlinēn*, from Proto-Germanic **hlināną* (“to lean, incline”), from Proto-Indo-European **ḱley-*.

senses.definition: The contract or deed under which such an interest is granted.
senses.example: The lease was signed Tuesday, granting the tenant exclusive use of the warehouse for five years.

senses.definition: The document containing such a contract or deed.
senses.example: Please bring a copy of the signed lease to the leasing office on Monday.

senses.definition: An interest granting exclusive use of any thing, such as a car or boat.
senses.example: We signed a three-year lease on a new car, so we'll never own it.

senses.definition: The period of such an interest.
Short for DHCP lease The temporary assignment of an IP address to a networked device.
senses.example: The router's DHCP lease for my laptop expired, so it lost its connection.

senses.definition: An open pasture or common.
senses.example: The cattle grazed on the village lease while the farmers tended their crops.

senses.definition: The place at which the warp-threads cross on a loom.
senses.example: The weaver checked the lease, where the warp threads cross, before starting the cloth.

senses.definition: An interest in land granting exclusive use or occupation of real estate for a limited period; a leasehold.
senses.example: The company holds a ninety-nine-year lease on the land beneath the shopping center.

senses.definition: To hold a lease as a tenant; to rent.
senses.example: I'm leasing a small apartment in Runcorn for a month while I'm there for work.

senses.definition: To assign a temporary IP address to (a networked device).
senses.example: The DHCP server will lease an address to any device that connects to the Wi-Fi.

senses.definition: To accept such an assignment of (an IP address).
senses.example: My laptop leases a new IP address each time it reconnects to the office network.

senses.definition: To gather.
senses.example: The women went out to lease the fields after the harvest.

senses.definition: To pick, select, pick out; to pick up.
senses.example: He leased the best fish from the net before anyone else arrived.

senses.definition: To glean.
senses.example: After the harvest, the poor were allowed to lease the remaining wheat from the field.

senses.definition: To glean, gather up leavings.
senses.example: The children followed the reapers to lease whatever grain the workers had dropped.

senses.definition: To grant a lease as a landlord; to let.
senses.example: Our landlord decided to lease the upstairs apartment to a young couple.

core.definition: A written contract that lets someone use property, such as an apartment, office, car or equipment, for a set period in exchange for regular payments.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long E and an unvoiced S, so it sounds like 'lees' and rhymes with 'cease' or 'peace'. Learners often add a vowel or voice the final sound, which makes it sound like 'leez'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is practical and business-like, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lease' mainly for long-term rentals, such as a one-year apartment lease, and for car leases. For short or informal arrangements, people usually say 'rent' or 'stay.' You can say 'I signed a lease' or 'My lease is up in June' in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Rent is the regular payment or the act of renting, while a lease is the contract that sets the terms, often for a longer, fixed period.
A sublease is a new agreement in which the original tenant rents the property to someone else, usually with the landlord's permission.

examples.everyday: We just signed a year-long lease on a two-bedroom near the park.
examples.professional: Please send the signed lease to facilities so we can finalize the office move by Friday.
examples.analytical: A lease transfers the right to possess property while the owner keeps title, which is why its terms must be spelled out so carefully.

nuance.analogy: A lease is like borrowing a room with a written promise: you get the key, and the owner keeps the house.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French lese, from Old French laissier, 'to let go, leave, allow.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'less' with a short vowel, or like 'leaze' with a voiced ending; use a long E and an unvoiced S.
Using 'lease' for a few days of lodging; 'rent' or 'stay' fits short arrangements better.

lease.etymology: From Middle English **lesen*, from Anglo-Norman **leser*, Old French *lesser*, *laisier* (“to let, let go”), partly from Latin *laxō* (“to loose”) and partly from Old High German *lāzan* (“to let, let go, release”), cognate with whence *let*.

conversation.text: Our lease is up in June, so we need to decide whether to stay.
Read the whole lease before you sign it.
We decided to lease a car instead of buying one.

senses.definition: To help or assist, especially voluntarily.
senses.example: If we all lend a hand, the work will go quickly.

core.definition: To help someone with a task or problem, usually by doing some of the work for them.

pronunciation.tip: Reduce 'a' to a quick 'uh', so the phrase flows as 'len-duh HAND'. Stress 'hand' most strongly.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests generosity and teamwork, and people usually say it when offering or requesting help in a friendly way.
nuance.usage_note: This is a very common American expression at home, at work, and in everyday talk. People often ask, 'Could you lend a hand?' or offer, 'Need a hand?' A natural reply is 'Sure, I'd be glad to,' or 'Thanks, I really appreciate it.' Use 'with' before the task, as in 'lend a hand with the move.'

distinctions.note: 'Pitch in' suggests several people joining a shared effort. 'Lend a hand' often refers to helping one person with a task.
'Help out' is broader and can be used for temporary or occasional help. 'Lend a hand' is more physical or practical in feel.

collocations: always willing to lend a hand
lend a hand with the move

examples.everyday: Could you lend a hand with these grocery bags? They're heavier than I thought.
examples.professional: If anyone has capacity this week, please lend a hand with the database migration, since we're behind schedule.
examples.analytical: Many ethicists argue that moral obligation grows when someone is in need and we are in a position to lend a hand.

nuance.analogy: Like holding the other end of a heavy couch so someone doesn't have to carry it alone.
nuance.etymology: 'Lend' comes from Old English lǣnan, and 'hand' from Old English hand.
common_mistakes: Omitting 'with' before the task, as in 'lend a hand the dishes' instead of 'lend a hand with the dishes'.
Saying 'borrow a hand', which is incorrect; 'lend' is the right verb for giving help.
Pronouncing 'a' as a full 'ay' sound instead of the reduced 'uh'.

senses.definition: Any compound formed from damage to a nucleic acid.
senses.example: Oxidative stress produced a lesion in the DNA that the repair enzymes later removed.

senses.definition: A wound or injury.
An infected or otherwise injured or diseased organ or part, especially such on a patch of skin.

Injury or an unfair imbalance in a commutative contract wherein the consideration is less than half of the market value, which then serves as a basis for the injured party to sue to rescind the agreement.
senses.example: The court found the contract voided for lesion, since the price was far below market value.

senses.definition: To wound or injure, especially in an experiment or other controlled procedure.
senses.example: Researchers lesioned the rats' motor cortex to study how movement recovers after injury.

core.definition: An area of abnormal or damaged tissue on the body, such as a sore, spot, growth or injured patch of skin or an organ.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending is /ʒən/, with the zh sound from 'measure', not the sh sound from 'nation'. Don't confuse it with 'lesson' (/ˈlɛsən/).

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals damage or disease, so it is used in a serious, clinical tone.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors, nurses, and patients use it in medical settings, for example 'a lesion on the liver' or 'the lesion is benign'. Outside medicine it sounds unusually technical. For everyday talk, Americans say 'sore', 'spot', 'bruise', or 'mark'. The verb sense, to injure in an experiment, is mainly used in research writing.

distinctions.note: A wound is an injury caused by an external force, such as a cut. A lesion is any abnormal area of tissue, whether from injury, infection, or disease.
A sore is an everyday word for an open or painful area on the skin. A lesion is the clinical term and can describe internal tissue too.

examples.everyday: The dermatologist looked at the spot on my arm and said it was a small lesion, but nothing to worry about.
examples.professional: The radiology report noted a two-centimeter lesion in the left lobe, so we need a follow-up scan before the trial starts.
examples.analytical: Whether a lesion counts as evidence of injury or as a normal variant depends on the diagnostic criteria the study uses.

nuance.analogy: Like a dent on a car panel: a localized area where the surface no longer matches the rest.
nuance.etymology: From Latin laesio, 'injury', from laedere, 'to injure'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'lesson' for 'lesion' (the vowel and ending differ).
Using 'lesion' for any everyday scratch; Americans would normally say 'cut' or 'scrape'.

lesion.etymology: From Middle English *lesioun* (“physical injuring of the body”), from Old French *lesion* (“hurt, offense, wrong, injury, wound”), from Latin *laesiō* (“hurt, harm, injury”) (whence *-ion* (“noun suffix denoting action, result, process, state,…

senses.definition: A vast sea monster of tremendous strength, either imaginary or real, described as the most dangerous and powerful creature in the ocean.
senses.example: Sailors told stories of a leviathan that could swallow an entire ship whole.

senses.definition: A thing which is monstrously great in size, strength, etc. (especially a ship); also, a person with great power or wealth.
senses.example: The new cruise ship is a leviathan that carries more passengers than many small towns.

senses.definition: Sometimes in the form Leviathan: based on the writings of Thomas Hobbes, the political state, especially a domineering and totalitarian one.
senses.example: Our seminar debated whether Hobbes's Leviathan justified a state with unlimited authority over citizens.

senses.definition: Synonym of Satan (“the supreme evil spirit in the Abrahamic religions, who tempts humanity into sin; the Devil”).
senses.example: The sermon warned that the Leviathan tempts believers toward pride and greed.

senses.definition: Very large; enormous, gargantuan.
senses.example: They bought a leviathan SUV that barely fit into the garage.

core.definition: A huge sea monster in the Bible and ancient myth; in general use, anything enormous and powerful, such as a giant ship or company.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VY, which is an 'eye' diphthong. The last syllable is weak, so say thun, and the middle vowels glide quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests overwhelming size or menace.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use leviathan in writing and speech for something huge and powerful, often a corporation, government, or ship, as in 'a tech leviathan.' It sounds literary, so in casual talk people more often say giant or monster. The political sense comes from Thomas Hobbes's book Leviathan (1651), which describes the state as an all-powerful body.

distinctions.note: Giant is an everyday word for something very large; leviathan is more literary and implies power or menace.
Behemoth is also a biblical word for a huge creature (Job 40); in modern use it also means an enormous company or thing.

examples.everyday: That new mall is a leviathan, and I always get lost inside it.
examples.professional: The merger made the company a leviathan that the regional banks struggle to compete with.
examples.analytical: Hobbes's Leviathan treats the sovereign state as an artificial person whose power keeps people from a war of all against all.

nuance.analogy: Like a whale in a small pond: it dwarfs everything around it.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew liwyatan, a sea monster; possibly from a root meaning 'to twist,' though the origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with extra syllables such as lee-VAY-uh-thee-un; say luh-VY-uh-thun.
Using leviathan as a casual word for anything big; it sounds literary or dramatic.
nuance.biblical_note: Leviathan (Hebrew liwyatan) is a sea monster in the Old Testament, often a symbol of chaos or of the enemies of God. Job 41 describes it in detail as untamable by human hands, and Job 3:8 suggests it may be stirred up by those who curse the day. Psalm 74:14 says God crushed the heads of Leviathan, and Isaiah 27:1 promises that the LORD will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent.

leviathan.etymology: The is derived from Middle English *leviathan,levyathan,levyethan*, from Late Latin *leviathan*, a of Biblical Hebrew *לִוְיָתָן*, possibly from *לִוְיָה* + *-תָּן*.

senses.definition: In a lewd manner.

core.definition: In a sexually suggestive or vulgar way, especially in a way that offends general standards of decency.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a light 'lee'. Many learners put equal stress on both syllables or make the ending sound like 'lee-DLY'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative, implying moral disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lewdly mainly in writing, reports or formal descriptions of behavior, such as a court record or a news story. In everyday speech they would more often say 'inappropriately' or 'in a crude way'. It is rarely used casually.

distinctions.note: Inappropriately is a broad, everyday word for not fitting the situation; lewdly specifically means sexually suggestive.
Crudely means in a rough or unrefined way, while lewdly focuses on sexual suggestion.

examples.everyday: He was asked to leave the party after he started talking lewdly to the waitress.
examples.professional: The report stated that the employee had acted lewdly during the off-site event, which led to a formal review.
examples.analytical: The text describes the characters who behave lewdly in the marketplace as signs of a community that has lost its moral bearings.

nuance.analogy: Acting lewdly is like wearing a shirt with a rude slogan in church: the message itself is the problem.
nuance.etymology: From lewd (see above) plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using lewdly to mean 'loudly' or 'loosely', which are different words.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, Greek words such as aselgeia, meaning licentiousness or unrestrained sensuality, are the sources behind English words for lewdness. The RSV uses terms such as licentiousness rather than lewdly, so this adverb is not a direct Bible term. Galatians 5:19 lists licentiousness among the works of the flesh, and Romans 13:13 warns against debauchery and licentiousness. These passages describe unrestrained sexual behavior as contrary to a life guided by the Spirit.

lewdly.etymology: From Middle English *lewedly* (“ignorantly, stupidly”); equivalent to *lewd* + *ly*.

senses.definition: One who uses bombastic or pretentious wording or language.

core.definition: A person who uses showy, pretentious or bombastic words to seem clever or important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAY, and the final -anes is pronounced neez, rhyming with 'knees.' The initial ph is a plain f sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It mocks someone who uses big words to impress rather than to communicate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use lexiphanes in conversation. It appears mainly in literary criticism, in wordplay or in an erudite joke about a pompous speaker. It is an insult, so using it to someone's face would sound harsh unless you are teasing an old friend. The common everyday alternatives are 'show-off' or 'windbag.'

distinctions.note: A pedant fussily insists on rules and details, while a lexiphanes uses showy vocabulary to impress. A person can be both.
A logophile loves words and enjoys them for their own sake. A lexiphanes uses fancy words in a way that often hides meaning.

collocations: a lexiphanes of the old school

examples.professional: The vendor's proposal read like the work of a lexiphanes, full of jargon that hid what the product would actually do.
examples.analytical: Lucian's satire of the Lexiphanes mocks the writer who mistakes ornate vocabulary for substance.

nuance.analogy: A lexiphanes is like someone who wears a tuxedo to a picnic: the outfit is impressive, but it works against the occasion.
nuance.etymology: From Greek lexiphanes 'one who shows off words,' from lexis 'word' and phainein 'to show.'
common_mistakes: Confusing lexiphanes with lexicographer, who writes dictionaries.
Pronouncing the final -anes as -uh-nez instead of -ayn-eez.

senses.definition: To establish a liaison.
senses.example: Our office will liaise with the county health department about vaccine distribution.

senses.definition: To act between parties with a view to reconciling differences.
senses.example: The mediator liaised between the two families until they agreed to a settlement.

senses.definition: To cooperate, consult and discuss in order to come to a common solution.
senses.example: Engineers and designers liaise weekly to make sure the app matches the specifications.

core.definition: To communicate and coordinate closely with another person or group so that work is done together smoothly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'AYZ', which rhymes with 'days'. Do not pronounce it with a short i in the first syllable or stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, describing cooperation in a work context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use liaise mostly at work, in emails, meetings and project updates, as in 'I will liaise with legal.' In casual speech they would often say 'work with' or 'coordinate with'. It can sound a bit formal or bureaucratic, so use it in professional settings rather than with friends.

distinctions.note: Coordinate is more general and focuses on organizing tasks; liaise emphasizes the communication link between two parties.
Collaborate means working together on the same task; liaise often means acting as the connection between groups who may work separately.

examples.everyday: I will liaise with the contractor so that the kitchen project stays on schedule.
examples.professional: I will liaise with the security team and the vendor, so we can close the ticket before Friday.
examples.analytical: A good translator must liaise between two traditions, carrying meaning across without imposing one framework on the other.

nuance.analogy: To liaise is to be the bridge between two shores: traffic moves across you, but you are not the destination.
nuance.etymology: Back-formation from liaison, from French liaison, from lier, 'to bind'.
common_mistakes: Using liaise without a preposition; the usual pattern is liaise with someone or between parties.
Pronouncing it as 'LAY-ize' with stress on the first syllable.

senses.definition: In a liberal manner; generously; freely.
senses.example: She sprinkled cinnamon liberally over the apple pie before baking it.

senses.definition: In accordance with political views associated with the liberals.
senses.example: Her senator votes liberally on most social issues, according to the voter guide.

core.definition: Generously or in large amounts; without holding back.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Americans reduce the middle syllable to a quick 'er' and pronounce the last syllable as 'lee'. Do not pronounce the 'a' as a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests generosity, though in political talk it refers to a different meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'liberally' in everyday speech with food or money, as in 'Season liberally with salt.' In politics, 'liberal' is a separate word, so 'liberally' can refer to liberal ideology, but context makes it clear. It sounds more formal than 'a lot' or 'generously.'

distinctions.note: Generously is more common in everyday speech and emphasizes kindness; liberally emphasizes abundance or freedom.
Lavishly suggests luxury or extravagance; liberally suggests plentiful but not necessarily luxurious amounts.

examples.everyday: Put the cheese on liberally, because the kids love it.
examples.professional: The donor gave liberally to the scholarship fund this year.
examples.analytical: The author uses images liberally throughout the chapter, creating a dense symbolic texture.

nuance.analogy: To use something liberally is to pour from a full pitcher rather than a dropper.
nuance.etymology: From 'liberal' (from Latin 'liberalis', 'of a free person') plus the adverbial suffix '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'liberally' (generously) with political liberal views without context.
Using it with 'a lot' in a redundant way, such as 'liberally a lot'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, 'liberally' translates Greek words meaning generosity. James 1:5 describes God giving to all generously and without reproach, using the Greek 'haplōs', meaning simply or generously. Deuteronomy 15:14 tells Israelites to furnish departing servants liberally from their flock and produce, reflecting the generous provision expected under God's law.

senses.definition: A fawning toady; a base sycophant.
senses.example: Everyone in the office knew the regional manager's lickspittle would agree with any idea he had.

senses.definition: The practice of giving empty flattery for personal gain.
senses.example: Her lickspittle at the board meetings earned her a seat on the committee.

senses.definition: To play the toady; take the role of a lickspittle to please (someone).
senses.example: Rather than defend his staff, the manager chose to lickspittle the vice president all afternoon.

1 2 “lick, v.” and “spittle, n.” listed in the Oxford English Dictionary, second edition (1989)

core.definition: A servile flatterer who fawns over powerful people in order to gain favors or advantages for himself.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, LIK. The final syllable is a syllabic l with no vowel, so say 'spit-l' as one smooth unit.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It insults someone as a spineless flatterer and is meant as a serious criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use lickspittle in daily speech. You will find it in political commentary, history books, editorials, or humorous writing about office politics. It is a strong insult, so using it in front of the person described can cause real offense. A more common everyday alternative is 'yes-man' or 'brown-noser'.

distinctions.note: A yes-man agrees with everything a boss says, while a lickspittle also flatters and grovels in a more servile, humiliating way.
Brown-noser is more informal and common in American workplaces, while lickspittle is more literary and harsher.

examples.everyday: My brother calls his coworker a lickspittle because he laughs at every one of the boss's jokes.
examples.professional: In the meeting, the director's lickspittle agreed with everything the CEO said without offering any analysis.
examples.analytical: Machiavelli's warning about courtiers reflects a long tradition in which the lickspittle gains favor by flattery rather than merit.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog that rolls over and wags for every treat, always eager to please the one holding the power.
nuance.etymology: Compound of lick and spittle, a picturesque image of groveling servility.
common_mistakes: Using it as a neutral word for a polite assistant; it is always an insult.
Spelling it as two words, 'lick spittle', in formal writing.

lickspittle.etymology: A compounding: *lick* (“pass one’s tongue over”) + *spittle* (“saliva”); the verb may derive by back-formation from the nominal derivation *lickspittling*.

senses.definition: The condition of being illuminated.
The relative whiteness or transparency of a color.
senses.example: The painter adjusted the lightness of the blue until it matched the afternoon sky.

senses.definition: The product of being illuminated.
senses.example: The lightness in the room came from a single skylight above the reading table.

senses.definition: The state of having little (or less) weight, or little force.
senses.example: Engineers praised the lightness of the new carbon frame, which made the bike easy to carry.

senses.definition: Agility of movement.
senses.example: The dancer's lightness on her feet amazed the judges during the final round.

senses.definition: Freedom from worry.
senses.example: After submitting the thesis, she felt a lightness she had not known in months.

senses.definition: Levity, frivolity; inconsistency.
senses.example: His lightness about the audit worried his manager, who needed someone to take it seriously.

core.definition: The quality of being bright or full of light; in color, how light or pale a shade looks compared with darker ones.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The t often blends into the n, so say LYT-nus, not LY-tuh-ness. The final -ness is a weak, reduced vowel.
