senses.definition: A path, sidewalk/pavement or other maintained place on which to walk.
senses.example: We cut across the park on the gravel walk behind the library.

senses.definition: A person's conduct or course in life.
senses.example: people of different ages and walks

senses.definition: A situation where all players fold to the big blind, as their first action (instead of calling or raising), once they get their cards.
senses.example: Everyone folded to the big blind, so the hand ended in a walk before the flop.

senses.definition: In coffee, coconut, and other plantations, the space between them.
senses.example: The workers cleared weeds from the walk between the rows of coffee bushes.

senses.definition: A sequence of alternating vertices and edges, where each edge's endpoints are the preceding and following vertices in the sequence. Compare path, trail.
senses.example: In our graph theory homework, the professor asked us to find a walk of length five between two vertices.

senses.definition: Something very easily accomplished; a walk in the park.
A check drawn on a bank that was not a member of the London Clearing and whose sort code was allocated on a one-off basis; they had to be "walked" (hand-delivered by messengers).
An Olympic Games track event requiring that the heel of the leading foot touch the ground before the toe of the trailing foot leaves the ground.
An award of first base to a batter following four balls being thrown by the pitcher; known in the rules as a "base on balls".
senses.example: The pitcher now has two walks in this inning alone.

senses.definition: (historical) A place for keeping and training puppies for dogfighting.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) An enclosed area in which a gamecock is confined to prepare him for fighting.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: To move on foot, setting one foot ahead of the other so that at least one foot is always touching the ground.

pronunciation.tip: The l is silent, so say 'wawk', not 'wawlk'. Many Americans pronounce it /wɑk/ because of the cot-caught merger, which is also correct.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is everyday and can also be used positively for healthy exercise or a relaxed outing.
nuance.usage_note: Walk is one of the most common words in American English, used for everything from a short stroll to a walk to work. Americans say go for a walk or take a walk, and they use hike for long walks in nature. Walk is also used for going somewhere on foot, as in I walked to the store, and a bus or car trip is never a walk.

distinctions.note: Stroll means to walk slowly and casually, usually for pleasure; walk is the general word.
Hike means a long walk, often over hills or trails in nature; walk can be any distance in any place.
Run means to move faster, with both feet off the ground at times; walk is slower and always has one foot down.

examples.everyday: Do you want to go for a walk after dinner?
examples.professional: I'll walk over to the data team's desk after the stand-up to go over the results.
examples.analytical: Philosophers from the Peripatetic school of Aristotle to modern phenomenologists have used walking as a model for thinking through problems.

nuance.analogy: Walking is like a pendulum: one foot swings forward while the other stays planted, and the body keeps moving.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wealcan, to roll or toss; the sense of moving on foot developed in Middle English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I walked by bus' or 'I walked by car'; in American English you take the bus or drive, and walk only means going on foot.
Adding an l sound, as in 'wawlk'; the l is silent.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the idea is halak, to walk, and in Greek it is peripateo, to walk about or conduct one's life. In Scripture walk often means a whole way of life. Micah 6:8 invites the people to walk humbly with their God, describing faithful conduct before God. Galatians 5:16 tells believers to walk by the Spirit, meaning to let the Spirit guide their daily conduct. Ephesians 4:1 urges the readers to lead a life worthy of their calling, which describes a Christian's conduct in the world.

walk.etymology: From Middle English *walk*, *walke*, *walken*, *walkyn*, *wolken* (“to roll, toss, or turn; to walk; to move; to be living; to beat or full; to perform”), a conflation of Old English *wealcan* (“to move around; to revolve; to roll; to fluctuate; to…

senses.definition: Any water that has been used in some human domestic or industrial activity and, as a result, now contains waste products.

core.definition: Water that has been used in homes or industry and now contains unwanted waste materials.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress is on WAYST and secondary stress on wah in the compound. The t in water is a flap that sounds like a soft d, so say 'WAH-der' rather than a hard 't'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical and environmental term, not an emotional one.
nuance.usage_note: Common in news, city government and environmental contexts. It covers used water from sinks, showers, toilets and factories. Gray water is lightly used household water that may be reused for irrigation, and sewage is wastewater that contains human waste. In everyday talk people often say 'sewage' or 'dirty water'.

distinctions.note: Sewage is wastewater that contains human waste; wastewater is the broader term, including industrial water and stormwater runoff.
Gray water is lightly used household water from sinks, showers and laundry that may be reused; wastewater is all used water.
Effluent is wastewater flowing out of a plant, pipe or process; it is a more specific technical term.

examples.everyday: The wastewater plant on the edge of town smells pretty bad when the wind blows from the east.
examples.professional: Our data pipeline ingests sensor readings from every wastewater treatment plant in the county.
examples.analytical: The regulation requires each factory to show that its industrial wastewater meets federal limits before discharge.

nuance.analogy: Like the dirty dishwater after washing a big dinner: used, mixed with grime, and no longer fit for drinking.
nuance.etymology: From waste (from Latin vastare 'to lay waste') and water (Old English wæter).
common_mistakes: Writing 'waste water' as two words in technical writing; the standard form is one word, wastewater.
Confusing wastewater with drinking water; wastewater is used water and is not safe to drink.
Putting the main stress on the second part of the compound, as in 'waste-WAH-ter'; the first syllable WAYST is stressed.

senses.definition: An instance or process of loss of strength.
A structural principle of mathematical logic that states that the hypotheses of any derived fact may be freely extended with additional assumptions.
senses.example: In the proof, weakening lets us add an unused assumption to the hypotheses without changing the conclusion.

core.definition: The process or instance of losing strength, power, or effectiveness over time.

pronunciation.tip: Three syllables, with the middle one reduced to a schwa. The final -ing is a short 'ing', not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it describes decline. It is neutral in technical contexts such as logic or materials.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech it describes gradual decline, as in 'the weakening of the dollar' or 'a weakening economy.' In logic and mathematics it names a specific inference rule. Americans say 'a weakening economy' rather than 'an economy in weakening.'

distinctions.note: Decline is a more general fall, often in numbers or quality; weakening specifically means losing strength or power.
Erosion is gradual wearing away, often of something physical or intangible; weakening can be sudden or gradual.

examples.everyday: The weakening of the dollar means my trip to Europe is getting more expensive.
examples.professional: We are seeing a weakening in demand for the enterprise tier, so I would rather not raise prices yet.
examples.analytical: Descartes's method of doubt aims at the weakening of prejudice before any firm foundation is built.

nuance.analogy: Like a battery draining slowly: nothing seems to happen at first, and then the phone suddenly shuts off.
nuance.etymology: From 'weaken' plus '-ing', from Old English wāc, meaning weak.
common_mistakes: Using 'weakening' as an adjective where 'weakened' is correct, as in 'a weakening immune system' for a damaged one.
Saying 'the weakening' to mean a weakened state; the noun names the process itself.

senses.definition: Directed with precision toward a specific target, purpose, or effect.

core.definition: Accurately directed at a target, or carefully aimed to have a specific effect, such as a remark or question.

pronunciation.tip: Aimed is a single syllable ending in a /md/ cluster, with no separate ed syllable. The stress falls on AIM, while well is lighter.

nuance.connotation: Positive for accuracy or skill. It can be negative when used for a remark that is pointed or cutting, such as a well-aimed jab.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use well-aimed for shots, throws, punches, and also for questions or comments that hit the target exactly. It is common in sports, politics, and everyday arguments. If someone makes a sharp remark, you might say that was a well-aimed comment, and a natural reply is Yeah, it stung a little.

distinctions.note: Accurate describes precision in general, while well-aimed focuses on how a shot, throw or remark was directed.
Well-timed refers to when something happens, while well-aimed refers to where or at what it is directed.
Well-targeted is common in marketing and advertising, whereas well-aimed is more general and conversational.

examples.everyday: That was a well-aimed snowball, right at the back of his neck.
examples.professional: Her well-aimed question during the review exposed a flaw in our assumptions about the data.
examples.analytical: The critic's well-aimed objection showed that the argument depended on a premise it never defended.

nuance.analogy: A well-aimed arrow hits the bull's-eye because the archer lined up the sight carefully before letting go.
nuance.etymology: Well (accurately) plus aim, from Old French esmer, to estimate or judge.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing aimed as two syllables (AY-med); it is one syllable, /eɪmd/.
Writing a shot well-aimed at the target as a model for the attributive form; in front of a noun, say a well-aimed shot.

senses.definition: Defined in an unambiguous and consistent way: specifically, such that any two objects implied to be identical are indeed identical.
senses.example: The function is well-defined, so every input produces exactly one output.

senses.definition: Having a clean and distinct outline.
senses.example: The lighthouse stood against the sky, its well-defined outline sharp in the morning light.

senses.definition: Accurately and precisely described or specified.
senses.example: The project manager wanted a well-defined scope before the team wrote any code.

core.definition: Defined clearly and precisely, so that its meaning or boundaries are unambiguous; in mathematics, a definition that gives one unique result.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable of defined, which is fyned, not DEE-fined. The first word gets a secondary stress, so say it as 'well' with a bit of emphasis.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests clarity and precision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use well-defined in both everyday and professional speech to say something has clear boundaries, such as 'a well-defined role' or 'a well-defined scope.' In math and computer science, it has a precise meaning: a definition that gives a single unambiguous result. Its opposite, ill-defined, is common in meetings to describe vague goals.

distinctions.note: Clear is general and everyday; well-defined emphasizes precise boundaries or structure.
Explicit describes something stated directly; well-defined describes its boundaries or structure, whether or not it is stated.

examples.everyday: Our kids have a well-defined bedtime routine, so the evenings go pretty smoothly.
examples.professional: Before we start the sprint, can we agree on a well-defined scope for the first milestone?
examples.analytical: A concept is well-defined only when every candidate instance can be unambiguously classified as belonging to it or not.

nuance.analogy: A well-defined term is like a property line surveyed and marked with stakes, so nobody can dispute where it ends.
nuance.etymology: Well (Old English wel) plus defined, from the Latin definire, to limit or set boundaries.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable of defined, as in DEE-fined.
Using it to mean well-known, which is a different idea.

senses.definition: Properly constructed or manufactured.
senses.example: This leather wallet is well-made, with double stitching that should last for years.

core.definition: Built or manufactured with good materials and careful workmanship, so it lasts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MADE, with light secondary stress on WELL. The vowel is the long a of late, and the d is a clear d sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises quality, durability and craftsmanship, and is used for products, furniture and clothing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use well-made for products they expect to last, as in 'a well-made chair' or 'a well-made car.' It is everyday language used in shops and reviews. For a more luxurious product, you might say high-quality or finely made.

distinctions.note: High-quality refers to a level of standard, often compared with others; well-made focuses on construction and craftsmanship.
Sturdy means strong and solid; well-made covers the whole construction, including finish and detail.

examples.everyday: These boots are well-made, so they'll last you a long time even with hard use.
examples.professional: Our engineers chose a well-made component that reduces warranty claims by a significant margin.
examples.analytical: The film is a well-made piece of storytelling, with a plot that rewards careful attention at every stage.

nuance.analogy: Like a good cabinet with straight joints and smooth drawers: you notice quality in how it works over years.
nuance.etymology: Well from Old English wel; made from Old English macian, 'to make, construct'.
common_mistakes: Writing well made without a hyphen before a noun, as in a well made chair.
Using well-made to describe a person's appearance; it describes things made by people.

senses.definition: Asking who is responsible for a task.

core.definition: Asking who will be responsible for managing or driving a task, project, or decision.

pronunciation.respelling: hooz TAY-king thuh LED ahn thiss
pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAY in 'taking' and on LED in 'lead', while 'the' and 'on' are reduced. The words 'taking the' link together as 'tay-king-thuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and businesslike. It is a clear, professional way to ask about ownership.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this in meetings, email threads, and project planning to find an owner for a task. A natural reply names the person, such as 'I'll take the lead on it,' or 'Priya is leading this one.' It is direct but not rude when asked in a team setting.

distinctions.note: To take charge implies full authority over a situation, while take the lead is more about driving a task forward.
To own something means to be fully accountable for it, which is a stronger commitment than take the lead.

collocations: take the lead on a project
take the lead on the report

examples.everyday: Who's taking the lead on planning the birthday party, you or your sister?
examples.professional: Who's taking the lead on this migration, Dev or Priya? We need one owner before Thursday.
examples.analytical: Who's taking the lead on this issue? A committee often diffuses responsibility, so naming one owner clarifies accountability.

nuance.analogy: Taking the lead is like the front runner in a group hike who sets the pace and chooses the trail.
nuance.etymology: Lead as a verb comes from Old English lǣdan, to guide or conduct.
common_mistakes: Saying 'take lead on this' without the article 'the', which sounds unnatural.
Using 'take the lead of' instead of 'take the lead on' when naming the task.
Confusing lead, pronounced with a short e, with the metal lead, which is the same spelling but a different word in use.

conversation.text: This is a big project. Who's taking the lead on this?

senses.definition: Showing enthusiastic and unconditional commitment; having no reservations.

core.definition: Showing complete, sincere enthusiasm and commitment, with no hesitation or reservations.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WHOLE, with a lighter secondary stress on HEART, so the second part should not be fully emphasized. Say the final -ed as a short 'id' sound, not as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises full, sincere commitment. It can also describe support that is total, which might be unrealistic, so it is best used when the support is genuine.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wholehearted most often in phrases like 'wholehearted support' or 'a wholehearted effort,' in workplaces, schools, sports, and public statements. It sounds slightly formal in casual talk, so in everyday conversation many people would just say 'I'm all in' or 'I'm totally for it.' Note that it is an adjective; to modify a verb, Americans use wholeheartedly.

distinctions.note: Half-hearted means lacking enthusiasm or effort, the opposite of wholehearted.
Sincere describes honest feelings or intentions, while wholehearted describes the degree of commitment or effort behind them.

examples.everyday: You have my wholehearted support for the picnic, so count me in.
examples.professional: The team gave wholehearted support to the revised deployment schedule.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's account of faith demands a wholehearted commitment that cannot be divided between God and personal comfort.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who gives every step full effort rather than jogging with one foot on the brake.
nuance.etymology: From whole and heart, from Old English hal and heorte.
common_mistakes: Using the adjective with a verb, as in 'I wholehearted agree' instead of 'I wholeheartedly agree.'
Writing it as 'whole-hearted' or 'wholeheart'; the standard spelling is one word, wholehearted.
Stressing WHOLE too weakly and placing equal stress on HEART.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew behind wholehearted is lev (heart, the center of will and thought) with shalem (complete, whole, sound), often describing an undivided devotion to God. Deuteronomy 6:5 commands Israel to love the LORD with all the heart, a call to undivided love that the New Testament repeats. Psalm 119:10 expresses the psalmist's wish to seek God with a whole heart and not wander from God's commandments. The Greek of Matthew 22:37 uses kardia (heart) for this same total devotion.

senses.definition: A pilot partner of another; a pilot who flies in the same wing or squadron.
senses.example: The lead pilot radioed his wingman to take the left flank during the training mission.

senses.definition: A friend or associate who accompanies one to offer (or receive) support, especially in flirting with love interests.
senses.example: Kevin asked his best friend to be his wingman at the party tonight.

senses.definition: To act as a wingman for (someone); to accompany in order to provide support.
senses.example: Jess offered to wingman her roommate at the bar so he could talk to the woman he liked.

core.definition: A friend who supports you socially, often by approaching someone you like or helping you get out of an awkward situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WING, and make the second syllable a short a as in 'man', not 'mun'. The word is one unit, so keep the two parts tight together.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can sound playful, but in dating contexts it sometimes carries an old-fashioned, gendered tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wingman' informally, especially for going out to bars or parties. The friend approaches someone you're interested in, or steps in to help you leave a bad conversation. A natural reply when asked is 'Sure, I've got your back.' The aviation sense is military and formal, while the social sense is casual.

distinctions.note: A sidekick is a regular companion in adventures or work, while a wingman is specifically a friend who helps with romance or social situations.
A best friend is a close personal bond in general, while a wingman has a specific social role at a particular event.

examples.everyday: Can you be my wingman tonight? I want to talk to that guy by the bar.
examples.professional: Our sales lead needs a wingman on the call to handle the technical questions while she focuses on the client.
examples.analytical: The idea of the wingman casts men as supports in romantic pursuit, and that framing reveals a lot about social expectations around courtship.

nuance.analogy: A wingman in an aviation squadron flies just off your wing, watching your back while you focus on the main task.
nuance.etymology: From military aviation, where a wingman flies beside and slightly behind a flight leader.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'mun' or 'min' instead of 'man' with a short a.
Using 'wingman' as an unmarked gendered term; 'wingwoman' is the more common word for a female friend in this role.

senses.definition: The spoils of a win; something, usually money, that has been won, usually by gambling.
senses.example: He tucked his winnings into his jacket and walked out of the casino.

core.definition: Money or prizes won, especially from gambling, a lottery or a contest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The plural ending is a voiced z, so it sounds like 'WIN-ingz', with the ng kept as in 'winning'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes money won, which can sound positive for a winner or negative in the context of compulsive gambling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always use winnings in the plural, even for one amount. It is common in talk about casinos, poker, sports betting and lotteries. Gambling winnings are taxable income in the United States, so the word often appears in tax discussions too. For money earned from work, people use earnings or pay.

distinctions.note: Winnings come from chance or contests; earnings come from work or investments.
A prize is the award a contest gives; winnings can be money from betting or any win.

examples.everyday: He cashed out his casino winnings and bought everyone dinner.
examples.professional: Gambling winnings must be reported as taxable income on the federal return, so keep your receipts.
examples.analytical: Winnings from chance are not earned in the way wages are, which complicates how we judge merit in a gambler's success.

nuance.analogy: Like a harvest from a field planted by luck instead of labor.
nuance.etymology: Plural of winning (noun), from Old English winnan, 'to struggle, gain'.
common_mistakes: Treating winnings as countable, such as 'three winnings', instead of saying 'three wins' or 'a lot of winnings'.
Using winnings for money earned from a job, where earnings is correct.

senses.definition: (This entry is a translation hub.)

core.definition: Only with great effort, and not easily; barely managing to do something.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable of difficulty. The middle syllables are weak, so say dif-ih-kul-tee quickly and lightly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests struggle, strain, or limited ability, though it does not necessarily sound dramatic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use with difficulty in everyday speech and in formal writing to describe effort, such as walking, reading, or breathing after an injury. It is often paired with managed to or barely. In casual talk people may also say barely or with a lot of trouble, but with difficulty sounds more precise and polite.

distinctions.note: Barely means almost not at all, while with difficulty describes success that required effort.
Hardly usually means almost never or scarcely, as in hardly ever, while with difficulty describes how something was achieved.

examples.everyday: After the surgery, my grandfather could get up from the chair only with difficulty.
examples.professional: The vendor's API handles large files, but it does so only with difficulty and frequent timeouts.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that the will acts with difficulty when it is divided against itself.

nuance.analogy: Like pushing a heavy cart uphill with one bad wheel: you move forward, but every step costs strain.
nuance.etymology: From Latin difficultas, from difficilis, meaning hard to do.
common_mistakes: Using the adjective difficult, as in with difficult, instead of the noun difficulty.
Dropping the middle syllables and saying dif-kult-ee, which makes the phrase sound clipped.

senses.definition: To come to a good understanding of.
senses.example: I still can't wrap my head around how the algorithm converged so quickly.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see wrap,‎ head,‎ around.
(uncommon) To crash into (something, especially a pole) messily and fatally while traveling in a motor vehicle.
senses.example: The drunk driver wrapped his head around a utility pole and died at the scene.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: To understand something complicated or difficult to grasp, after thinking about it hard.

pronunciation.tip: The verb wrap is silent on the w, and 'one's' reduces to a quick 'wunz'. Stress falls on 'around', the final syllable of the phrase, and words run together so 'wrap one's' sounds almost like 'rap-wunz'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative, typically used when an idea is hard to understand, as in 'I can't wrap my head around it.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in casual and professional conversation to talk about struggling with a new concept, a surprising decision, or a complicated plan. It usually appears in negative or question form, such as 'I still can't wrap my head around this.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, it's a lot to process.'

distinctions.note: Understand is neutral and general, while wrap one's head around suggests effort to grasp something difficult or counterintuitive.
Get is very informal and quick, while wrap one's head around implies a larger, more effortful struggle.

collocations: can't wrap my head around it
hard to wrap your head around
wrap your head around a concept

examples.everyday: I still can't wrap my head around how she moved to Alaska without telling anyone.
examples.professional: Our stakeholders are still trying to wrap their heads around the new pricing model.
examples.analytical: Readers often struggle to wrap their heads around the paradox the author presents in the opening chapter.

nuance.analogy: It is like trying to hold a huge, awkward idea in your mind until it fits.
nuance.etymology: Idiomatic, from the literal sense of wrapping cloth around the head, later used figuratively for mental effort.
common_mistakes: Using the literal sense, as if you were physically wrapping something around your head.
Omitting the word one's or using the wrong possessive, such as 'wrap the head around it' instead of 'wrap your head around it'.
Pronouncing one's as 'one-s' instead of the reduced 'wunz'.

senses.definition: An often humid, yellowish froth produced by fermenting malt worts, and used to brew beer, leaven bread, and also used in certain medicines.
senses.example: The brewer skimmed the yeast off the top of the fermenting wort before bottling the beer.

senses.definition: A single-celled fungus of any of a wide variety of taxonomic families.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the yeast cells looked like tiny budding ovals floating in the sample.

senses.definition: A true yeast or budding yeast in order Saccharomycetales.
senses.example: Genomic studies of the budding yeast Saccharomyces help researchers model human cell division.

senses.definition: Baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae)
senses.example: My grandmother still proofs yeast in warm water before she mixes the cinnamon rolls.

senses.definition: A compressed cake or dried granules of this substance used for mixing with flour to make bread dough rise.
senses.example: Add one packet of dry yeast to the flour and let the dough rise for an hour.

senses.definition: Brewer's yeast, certain species of Saccharomyces, principally Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces carlsbergensis.
senses.example: She mixes a spoonful of brewer's yeast into her smoothie for extra B vitamins every morning.

senses.definition: Candida, a ubiquitous fungus that can cause various kinds of infections in humans.
senses.example: Her doctor found yeast in the culture and prescribed an antifungal cream for the rash.

senses.definition: The resulting infection, candidiasis.
senses.example: After the antibiotics, he developed a yeast infection that itched for nearly two weeks.

senses.definition: A frothy foam.
senses.example: The yeast on the surface of the cider looked like a thick, creamy foam.

senses.definition: To ferment.
senses.example: The apple juice began to yeast after two days in the crock.

senses.definition: To rise.
senses.example: Let the dough yeast in a warm place until it doubles in size.

senses.definition: To exaggerate.
senses.example: Don't yeast the story, Mike; we all know the fish was maybe a foot long.

core.definition: A tiny single-celled fungus used to make bread rise and to ferment beer, wine and other drinks.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a long 'ee' sound, the same as in 'east'. The final 't' is a light, unreleased sound at the end of the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans buy yeast at grocery stores in packets or jars, and many people use it at home for bread and pizza dough. In baking, 'active dry yeast' and 'instant yeast' are the common types. Yeast is a neutral, everyday word, but in Scripture and sermons it can symbolize corruption.

distinctions.note: Leaven is a general word for anything that makes dough rise, including yeast; yeast is the specific living fungus.
Baking soda is a chemical leavening agent that reacts with acid; yeast is living and needs time to ferment dough.

examples.everyday: I forgot to buy yeast, so we're making flatbread instead of pizza tonight.
examples.professional: The bakery switched to instant yeast, which cut the proofing time in half for our sourdough line.
examples.analytical: Yeast converts sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide, which is why it was historically both a food agent and a symbol of transformation.

nuance.analogy: Like a tiny crowd of workers inside the dough, quietly producing gas that makes everything expand.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gist or gyst, meaning yeast or foam from fermentation.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'yest' with a short vowel
Using 'yeast' as a count noun in the plural when speaking of a single kind of yeast, as in 'three yeasts'
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, leaven (Hebrew se'or, שְׂאֹר; Greek zymē, ζύμη) often means yeast and symbolizes corruption or spreading influence. Exodus 12:15 commands Israel to remove leaven from their houses during the feast of unleavened bread. Matthew 16:6 warns the disciples to beware the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, which Jesus later explains as their teaching. Luke 13:21 uses leaven in the parable of the kingdom, where a small amount works through the whole dough, showing the hidden and growing power of God's kingdom.

traditions.view: The Orthodox use leavened bread (prosphora) for the Eucharist, seeing leaven as a sign of life and the resurrection.
The Latin Church uses unleavened bread (azyme) for the Eucharist, while Eastern Catholic churches use leavened bread, following Orthodox practice.
Most Protestant churches use ordinary bread, often leavened, for the Lord's Supper; Lutheran and Anglican churches generally use leavened bread, while some Reformed communities use unleavened wafers.

yeast.etymology: From Middle English *yest*, *yeest*, *gest*, *gist*, from Old English *ġist*, *ġyst*, from **jestu*, from Proto-Germanic **jestuz*.

senses.definition: That is very true.

core.definition: That is very true; I completely agree, said with emphasis after someone says something strong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on say and gen, while you, can and that are reduced in fast speech, so it sounds like yoo-kun-SAY-thut-uh-GEN.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm, showing agreement, sometimes playful. It can sound sarcastic if the tone is flat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in casual conversation to strongly agree, especially when someone complains about heat, traffic, or prices. Good replies include tell me about it or simply a laugh. Avoid it with a boss in formal settings, where I agree is safer.

distinctions.note: Neutral and polite, while you can say that again is stronger and more informal.
A similar casual agreement, implying you have experienced the problem yourself.

examples.everyday: This heat is brutal. You can say that again, I'm melting out here.
examples.professional: The deadline is impossible with this team. You can say that again, we need more engineers.
examples.analytical: When the critic called the policy unworkable, the audience responded with a knowing you can say that again.

nuance.analogy: Like an echo that repeats the strongest point so everyone hears it clearly.
common_mistakes: Saying you can say it again; the phrase uses that, not it.
Using it sarcastically without a clear tone, which can confuse listeners.

conversation.text: "This traffic is terrible." "You can say that again."
"That meeting could have been an email." "You can say that again!"
"It's so hot today." "You can say that again."
"That was a long meeting." "You can say that again."
"Gas is so expensive these days." "You can say that again."

senses.definition: The quality or state of being young.
senses.example: Her youth and beauty attracted him to her.

senses.definition: The part of life following childhood; the period of existence preceding maturity or age; the whole early part of life, from childhood, or, sometimes, from infancy, to adulthood.
senses.example: Make the most of your youth, it will not last forever.

senses.definition: A young person.
senses.example: There was a group of youths hanging around the parking lot, reading fashion magazines and listening to music.

senses.definition: A young man; a male adolescent or young adult.
senses.example: The youth ran across the parking lot to catch the bus before it left.

senses.definition: Young persons, collectively.
senses.example: The youth of the town gathered at the park to clean up the riverbank.

core.definition: The period of life between childhood and adulthood, or young people considered as a group.

pronunciation.tip: End with a voiceless th, as in 'tooth', not a voiced th like 'this'. The vowel is a long 'oo' sound with a light y glide at the start.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing the energy and promise of young people, but negative when used in phrases like 'troubled youth' or 'youth crime'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'youth' in organizational settings, such as 'youth group', 'youth pastor' or 'youth soccer'. In everyday talk, 'teens', 'kids' or 'young people' is more natural. Saying 'the youth of today' sounds old-fashioned or preachy.

distinctions.note: 'Adolescence' is a technical term for the developmental stage from puberty to adulthood, while 'youth' is a broader, everyday word.
'Childhood' refers to the earlier years before youth, while 'youth' refers to the later part of the young years.
'Youth' can be a state or a group, while 'youngster' refers to one young person.

examples.everyday: We spent most of our youth in a small town outside Dayton.
examples.professional: Our youth program needs a volunteer coordinator who can work with teenagers on weekends.
examples.analytical: Philosophers since Aristotle have treated youth as the period when character is formed by habit and shaped by the company one keeps.

nuance.analogy: Youth is like spring in the year of a life: full of growth and energy, but not yet the harvest.
nuance.etymology: From Old English geogoþ, from geong 'young' with the abstract suffix -th.
common_mistakes: Voicing the final th so it sounds like 'yooth' with a /ð/ ending; keep it voiceless, like 'tooth'.
Using 'a youth' for a small child; it usually suggests a teenager or young man.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture speaks often of youth as a time to remember God and to be shaped by wisdom. Ecclesiastes 12:1 urges people to remember their Creator in the days of their youth, using the Hebrew phrase for youthful years, ne'urim. Psalm 71:5 describes trust in God as going back to one's youth, and 1 Timothy 4:12 tells young Timothy that no one should despise his youth, though he must set an example in speech and conduct.

youth.etymology: From Middle English *youthe*, *youghte*, *ȝouþe*, from Old English *ġeoguþ* (“the state of being young; youth”), from **juwunþa*, from Proto-Germanic **jugunþō*, **jugunþiz* (“youth”), corresponding to *young* + *-th*.

senses.definition: In the manner of a zealot; zealous; fanatic.

core.definition: Behaving in the manner of a zealot; fanatically devoted to a cause, belief, or group, and often intolerant of others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LAH. The first syllable is reduced, and the final ic sounds like 'ik'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying fanatical or intolerant behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Zealotic is rare in American speech and writing; Americans usually say zealous, fanatical, or 'a zealot' instead. You may see it in essays or literary criticism. In everyday talk, use fanatical or zealous for the same idea.

distinctions.note: Zealous can be neutral or positive, while zealotic is always critical and suggests fanatical extremism.
Fanatical is the common everyday word for excessive devotion, while zealotic is rare and more literary.

examples.professional: The team leader grew zealotic about the old process and rejected every suggestion for change.
examples.analytical: The author describes a zealotic loyalty that treats doubt as betrayal and dissent as heresy.

nuance.analogy: Zealotic conduct is like a guard who sees every visitor as an intruder and refuses to hear explanations.
nuance.etymology: Formed from zealot with the adjective suffix -ic.
common_mistakes: Using zealotic in casual speech where fanatical or zealous is more natural.
Confusing zealotic with zealous; zealotic carries a more negative sense.

senses.definition: Allowing selection from a fixed list of individually priced options shown on the menu.
senses.example: The restaurant had a huge à la carte menu and four specials that day.

senses.definition: Selective; only choosing what one likes or desires.
senses.example: Her approach to the company's policies is à la carte, following only the rules she likes.

senses.definition: By ordering individually priced items from the menu.
senses.example: We ordered the salad and the soup à la carte rather than the fixed-price dinner.

core.definition: Ordered as separately priced items from the menu, rather than as a fixed-price meal with several courses.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, KAHRT, and the "r" is pronounced in American English. The "la" is weak, like "luh," so avoid giving it a full "lah" sound. The final "t" is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes how a meal is ordered and often implies that the total cost will be higher or more flexible.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this at restaurants, especially when they want to order individual dishes instead of a set menu or combo. You might say "Can I get the salmon à la carte?" A typical reply from the server is "Sure, that's no problem." The phrase is also used figuratively to mean choosing only the parts of something you like.

distinctions.note: A prix fixe menu has a set price for several courses, while à la carte items are each priced separately.
A combo is a fast-food bundle with a fixed price, whereas à la carte means ordering each item on its own.

collocations: pick and choose à la carte

examples.everyday: We're not really hungry, so let's just order a couple of appetizers à la carte.
examples.professional: Our catering team offers a set package, but clients can also order à la carte if they want fewer items.
examples.analytical: The à la carte model lets customers choose freely, but it can make a meal's total cost harder to predict than a fixed-price menu.

nuance.analogy: Like ordering individual songs from a playlist instead of buying a whole album.
nuance.etymology: French, meaning "according to the card" or "according to the menu."
common_mistakes: Dropping the accent and writing "a la carte" in formal writing, which is acceptable in US usage but less correct in academic writing.
Stressing the first syllable of "carte" instead of the last.
Saying "à la carte" to mean a cheap meal; it refers to the way items are ordered, not their price.

conversation.text: You can get the full dinner, or order everything à la carte.
The sides are à la carte, so they cost extra.
Ordering à la carte ended up being more expensive than the combo.
